availableCommands.name: dataviz
availableCommands.description: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".

availableCommands.name: update-config
availableCommands.description: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.

availableCommands.name: verify
availableCommands.description: Verify that a code change actually does what it's supposed to by exercising it end-to-end and observing behavior — drive the affected flow, not just tests or typecheck. Run before committing nontrivial changes; bootstraps this repo's project verify skill if none exists yet. Don't invoke it on a diff that only touches tests, docs, or other code with no runtime surface to drive (a change to product source always has one) — there's nothing to observe.

availableCommands.name: doctor
availableCommands.description: Health-check the user's Claude Code setup and fix issues: diagnose installation health — what the `claude doctor` terminal diagnostics cover — from local data (duplicate or leftover installs, PATH, unparseable settings files, broken or colliding agent definitions); find unused skills, MCP servers, and plugins versus their context cost and disable dead weight; deduplicate local CLAUDE.md files against checked-in ones; trim checked-in CLAUDE.md files by cutting content a session could derive from the codebase (directory layouts, tech-stack lists, architecture overviews) while keeping gotchas, rationale, and non-standard conventions; migrate always-loaded CLAUDE.md guidance into lazy skills and nested CLAUDE.md files; flag slow hooks and context-heavy extensions; check the installed version is current; make auto mode the default permission mode; and pre-approve frequently denied read-only commands. Use when the user asks for a doctor run, checkup, audit, tune-up, or cleanup of their Claude Code setup or configuration.

availableCommands.name: loop
availableCommands.description: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace.

availableCommands.name: claude-api
availableCommands.description:
Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).

1	//! Draft `agent-runtime.v0` message types.
2	//!
3	//! The logical protocol multiplexes two kinds of traffic over one stream:
4	//! runtime/agent lifecycle events and ACP conversation traffic. Each
5	//! direction has its own envelope - [`ToRuntimeMessage`] for Agent Service to
6	//! Agent Runtime traffic and [`ToServerMessage`] for the reverse -
7	//! discriminated by a `"type"` field. Only the wrapped ACP payload is itself
8	//! a JSON-RPC message; the outer envelope is not.
9	//!
10	//! A connection hosts exactly one agent execution, so nothing on this schema
11	//! needs an agent or agent-instance identifier: [`AcpMessage`] simply carries
12	//! the agent's raw ACP traffic.
13	
14	use agent_client_protocol::RawJsonRpcMessage;
15	use serde::{Deserialize, Deserializer, Serialize, Serializer};
16	use specta::Type;
17	use specta_typescript::Unknown;
18	
19	#[cfg(test)]
20	mod test;
21	
22	/// The kind of runtime or agent state transition reported to the Agent Service.
23	///
24	/// The protocol does not define a full event-name catalog yet, so this enum
25	/// is non-exhaustive: unrecognized wire strings still round-trip losslessly
26	/// through [`SystemEvent::Unknown`]. [`SystemEvent::AcpReady`] is the one
27	/// name the Agent Service actually acts on (see
28	/// `agent_proxy::inbound::runtime::RuntimeConnectionDriver`, which waits for
29	/// it before starting the ACP `initialize`/`session/new` handshake) rather
30	/// than merely forwarding it for observability.
31	///
32	/// This has a hand-written [`Serialize`]/[`Deserialize`] impl rather than a
33	/// derive, so it cannot derive [`specta::Type`] either: nothing here
34	/// introspects its shape for TypeScript. Every field that carries a
35	/// `SystemEvent` is instead given a `#[specta(type = String)]` override at
36	/// the field, matching the plain string it actually serializes as.
37	#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq, Hash)]
38	#[non_exhaustive]
39	pub enum SystemEvent {
40	    /// The Agent Runtime's hosted agent process is up and its ACP channel is
41	    /// wired end-to-end: the Agent Service may now start the ACP
42	    /// `initialize`/`session/new` handshake. Sent at most once per
43	    /// connection, before any ACP traffic.
44	    AcpReady,
45	    /// An application-defined event name with no protocol-level meaning yet.
46	    Unknown(String),
47	}
48	
49	impl SystemEvent {
50	    /// Borrow the wire string for this event name.
51	    #[must_use]
52	    pub fn as_str(&self) -> &str {
53	        match self {
54	            Self::AcpReady => "acp_ready",
55	            Self::Unknown(name) => name,
56	        }
57	    }
58	}
59	
60	impl Serialize for SystemEvent {
61	    fn serialize<S>(&self, serializer: S) -> Result<S::Ok, S::Error>
62	    where
63	        S: Serializer,
64	    {
65	        serializer.serialize_str(self.as_str())
66	    }
67	}
68	
69	impl<'de> Deserialize<'de> for SystemEvent {
70	    fn deserialize<D>(deserializer: D) -> Result<Self, D::Error>
71	    where
72	        D: Deserializer<'de>,
73	    {
74	        Ok(match String::deserialize(deserializer)?.as_str() {
75	            "acp_ready" => Self::AcpReady,
76	            name => Self::Unknown(name.to_owned()),
77	        })
78	    }
79	}
80	
81	/// One complete ACP JSON-RPC message routed between the Agent Service and the
82	/// single agent execution hosted by this connection.
83	///
84	/// Its own JSON-RPC fields are opaque to TypeScript consumers here (typed as
85	/// an arbitrary object of unknown values): they already have a proper ACP SDK
86	/// on the TypeScript side, so this crate only needs to guarantee the message
87	/// round-trips unchanged. This is typed as a map rather than plain `unknown`
88	/// because [`ToRuntimeMessage`]/[`ToServerMessage`] carry it in an internally
89	/// tagged `Acp` variant, which requires its payload provably serialize as an
90	/// object so the `"type"` tag can be merged into it. `#[serde(transparent)]`
91	/// changes nothing about the actual wire format here - a single-field tuple
92	/// struct already serializes transparently by default - but it does tell
93	/// specta's serde-compatibility checker that this newtype is transparent, so
94	/// it looks through to the map type below instead of treating `AcpMessage`
95	/// itself as an opaque, non-mergeable struct.
96	#[derive(Debug, Clone, Serialize, Deserialize, Type)]
97	#[serde(transparent)]
98	pub struct AcpMessage(
99	    #[specta(type = std::collections::HashMap<String, Unknown>)] pub RawJsonRpcMessage,
100	);
101	
102	/// Agent Service to Agent Runtime traffic on the logical protocol stream.
103	#[derive(Debug, Clone, Serialize, Deserialize, Type)]
104	#[serde(tag = "type", rename_all = "camelCase")]
105	#[non_exhaustive]
106	pub enum ToRuntimeMessage {
107	    /// An ACP message routed to the hosted agent.
108	    Acp(AcpMessage),
109	}
110	
111	/// Agent Runtime to Agent Service traffic on the logical protocol stream.
112	#[derive(Debug, Clone, Serialize, Deserialize, Type)]
113	#[serde(tag = "type", rename_all = "camelCase")]
114	#[non_exhaustive]
115	pub enum ToServerMessage {
116	    /// An ACP message routed from the hosted agent.
117	    Acp(AcpMessage),
118	    /// A runtime or agent lifecycle event.
119	    Event {
120	        /// The event name.
121	        #[specta(type = String)]
122	        event: SystemEvent,
123	    },
124	}

content.text: Read the relevant code. Short answer: **the gating logic is easy (~10 lines); the cost is structural pl

umbing in `agent_harness`, roughly a half-day.**

## What already exists

`agent_proxy` does exactly this today
— `crates/agent_proxy/src/inbound/runtime.rs:123-147` waits for `SystemEv
ent::AcpReady` on the event channel and only then spawns `handle_agent_connected` (which runs `
initialize`/`session/new`). The comment there is even the rationale you just described. So there's a proven pattern to

copy.

## What's missing in `agent_harness`

Three things block a direct copy:

1. **No initialize at all.** `AgentSessionImpl` (
`domain/agent_sessions/session.rs:34-40`) is a pass-through `send`/`rece
ive` over the transport. Nothing in the harness sends an ACP handshake yet, so "wait,

then initialize" means writing the initialize half too.

2. **`create_session` is sync.** `AgentSessionManager::create_session(&mut self
, &AgentSessionId) -> &T` (`manager.rs:11`) can't await. Any waiting version either makes it `

async` or moves the wait behind the session.

3. **Receive is pull-based and single-consumer.** `session.receive()` reads the
raw transport directly. If creation loops on `recv()` waiting for the `Event`, it sw
allows any `Acp` frames that arrive first, and nobody else can read concurrently. You need a dem
ux — one loop draining the transport, routing `Event{..}` → read

iness signal, `Acp(..)` → the ACP side.

## Cheapest path

Don't hand-roll the demux —
`agent_runtime_protocol::domain::connection::ServerConnection::connect` (`connection/mod.rs:59`) already does it: give
it the channel and a `SystemEventHandler`, get back a real `agent_client_protocol::Channel`.

Your handler flips a `tokio::sync::watch<bool>` on `AcpReady`.

Then pick where the wait lives:

- **G
ate inside the session** (recommended): `create_session` stays sync and returns immediately; `send()` aw
aits the ready watch before writing, and the pump fires initialize once on
the ready edge. Callers never see the gate, tests stay synchronous-ish. ~60–80

lines.
- **Async `create_session`**: smaller diff (~30 lines) but the manager blocks on a container that may never bo

ot, and you need a timeout + a story for a container that dies pre-ready.

One open
question that decides the shape: should `send()` on a not-yet-ready session **
await**, **queue** (agent_proxy durably queues, per `service.rs:138-142
`), or **error**? Which do you want?

content.text: Scoped it.

`agent_proxy` isn't just a crate — it's a deployed vertical slice. Here's the full surface:

## What

"delete agent_proxy" actually touches

**Rust (safe, reversible via

git)**
- `crates/agent_proxy` — 19 files, 3,790 lines (929-line domain service + 1

,073-line test file)
- `services/agent_proxy_service` — 168 lines, the only reverse-dep of the lib
-

2 entries in root `Cargo.toml`, plus `Cargo.lock`
- `crates/mac
ro_service_urls/src/lib.rs:540-544` — the `wss://agent-proxy{-dev}

.macro.com` runtime URL
- 3 `.sqlx/query-*.json` cache entries

**Generated / c

ross-language**
- `packages/sdk`: `'agent-proxy'` in the service union (`config.ts:18`),
3 base URLs, `services.ts`, `specs/agent-proxy.json` — **this is a breaking change for

SDK consumers**
- `apps/web/src/lib/service-clients/service-agent-proxy/` — 39 generated files + an
`orval.config.ts` entry. Good news: **zero hand-written web code imports it**, so it's a

pure generated-artifact delete.
- `.github/workspace-dep-closures.json`, `docker/docker-compose.yml`

, `docker/Dockerfile.dev`, `infra/local/generated/acp/*`

**Deployed state — I won't touch this without an

explicit go**
- `infra/stacks/agent-proxy-service/` has `Pulumi.dev.yaml` **and `
Pulumi.prod.yaml`** — there's a live prod service. Deleting the stack source orphans real

cloud resources; they need `pulumi destroy` first, by you.
- `infra/stacks/dopp

ler-projects/index.ts` has an agent-proxy project.
- `crates/macro_db_client/migrations/20260729
215917_agent_proxy_pending_messages.sql` — **already applied**. Deleting an applied migration breaks every

environment's migration ledger. The right move is a new `DROP TABLE` migration, not a file delete.

## Two things

worth deciding before I start

1. **`agent_harness` is not close to parity.** Its wh
ole domain is ~200 lines of session/container scaffolding. `agent_proxy` carries the ACP hand
shake, the `AcpReady` gate you just asked about, the pending-message queue, turn accumulation, chat persistence, and 5 HTTP routes
(`/agents`, `/sessions/{id}/acp`, `/runtime` WS upgrade). Deleting it
now also deletes the reference implementation for the feature in your previous message. Only
doc comments in `agent_harness` reference it — no code

coupling — so it can stay around harmlessly while you port.

2. **Scope.** Which

do you want?
   - **(a) Full teardown now** — everything above except
infra-destroy and the migration, which I'd stage as a drop-migration and

a written handoff for you to run.
   - **(b) Code-only** — delete the crate + service +
Cargo/SDK/web wiring, leave `infra/` and the migration entirely alone for a later

pass.
   - **(c) Port first** — I lift the `AcpReady` gate and hand

shake into `agent_harness`, get it working, *then* we delete.

My
read is **(c) then (a)** — but if `agent_harness_service` is already the intended repl
acement and you just want the dead weight gone, (b) is a clean single commit. Which way

-- One row per message exchanged on an agent session's logical protocol
-- stream (see agent_runtime_protocol::domain::schema::v0 and
-- agent_session::domain::model::{Message, AgentSessionLog}). direction +
-- content together round-trip the Message enum (ToServer/ToRuntime); user_id
-- is set only when the entry is ACP traffic that originated from a user.
CREATE TABLE agent_session_log (
    id                UUID        PRIMARY KEY,
    agent_session_id  UUID        NOT NULL REFERENCES agent_session(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
    user_id           TEXT,
    direction         TEXT        NOT NULL CHECK (direction IN ('to_server', 'to_runtime')),
    content           JSONB       NOT NULL,
    created_at        TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

-- list_by_session reads a session's log in chronological order.
CREATE INDEX agent_session_log_session_order
    ON agent_session_log (agent_session_id, created_at, id);

content.text: Read it all. Good news first: **`agent_session`
is already shaped for this.** `AgentSessionLog { agent_session_id, user_id, content: Message }` with
`Message::ToServer | ToRuntime` persisted as `direction` + `content` JSONB round-trips wh
ole protocol envelopes losslessly. You're not designing the persistence model — it exists. What

you're deciding is what it *means*.

Here's what I think the real questions are.

## 1. Is the log the

source of truth, or an audit trail?

This is the fork everything else hangs off.

`agent_proxy` had `translate.rs` + `
TurnAccumulator` because ACP arrives as a stream of deltas and ch
at needs coherent messages. If you delete the proxy, that fold has to live
*somewhere* — you've moved it, not removed it. Three places

it can go:

- **Client-side fold.** Log is truth, UI replays ra
w ACP. Cleanest server, but ACP semantics le

ak into the frontend and every client reimplements the fold.
- **Derived projection.** Log is truth,
a projector writes a read model. Most work, best reads, and repl

ayable when the fold logic changes.
- **In-memory fold + snapshot.** Log is the write
-ahead record, live state is memory, periodic snapshot. Fast, but a rest

art mid-turn has to replay.

Which one do you have in mind? I'd guess you're le
aning at the first, and it's defensible for a coding agent where the "

chat" is really a transcript.

## 2. Volume — this is the one that'll bite

ACP `session/update`
notifications stream at roughly token granularity. One `INSERT` per envelope means **thousands of rows per turn**, each with a J
SONB payload, on the hot path of a live stream. `AgentSessionLogRepo::create` is one

-row-at-a-time with no batching.

Do you want *literally* all ACP, or all ACP *except* stre
aming deltas? "Persist every request/response and every terminal notification, drop the intermediate text ch
unks" gets you 95% of the replay value at 1% of the rows. If you do want the
deltas, this needs batched or async-buffered writes before

it goes near production.

## 3. Ordering is currently broken for this use

case

`agent_session_log` orders by `(created_at, id)` — and `id` is a random UUID.
Two rows written in the same microsecond tie-break **randomly**, which for a token stream means
scrambled output. You need a monotonic `BIGSERIAL seq` (or per
-session counter) as the real order key. Small migration, but it's load-bearing the moment the

log becomes the transcript.

## 4. What still reaches the channel thread?

`
AgentSession` keeps `created_from_thread_id` *and* its own `thread_id`. So a comms thread still exists — me
aning "no longer proxy to chat" presumably means *no chat-message proxy crate*, not *no thread output
*. Someone still has to post something human-readable into that thread when the agent repl
ies. Is that a thin projector off the log, or does the agent explicitly emit "post

this to the thread" actions?

## 5. Does the log make sessions resumable?

If a container d
ies mid-session, can you spawn a new one and replay the log into it to reconstit
ute state? If **yes**, the log must be complete and exact, and that kills the fil
tering idea in #2. If **no** — it's a transcript, resume is the harness's problem via
`acp_session_id` — you have much more freedom. This one constrains #2, so it's worth answ

ering first.

---

My instinct: **log everything except streaming text deltas, add
a `seq` column, fold client-side, treat resume as out of scope for v1.** But #5 is the question
that decides it — where's your head at on resumability?

a consequence.

## The black box has one hole: `user_id` attribution

`AgentSessionLog.user_id` is `Some` only
when the ACP originated from a user. If persistence is a side effect of `LiveAgentSession::send`, then `send()` has to

know *who* — and today it takes only a message.

So the black box can't be fully bl

ind. Either:

```rust

<'static>>, message: ToRuntimeMessage) -> ...
```

or two doors — `send(msg)` for har

the second: the call sites genuinely are two different things (a user prompt v

so it stays clean either way.

## `create` flexibility — what I think you actually need
Four pressures on that trait, in the order they'll hur

are implied by the owner, not passed in
    fn append(&self, entry: NewLogEntry) -> impl Future<Output =

Result<LogSeq>> + Send;

    fn append_many(&self, entries: Vec<NewLogEntry>) -> impl Future<Output = Result<L
ewLogEntry` instead of `AgentSessionLog`** — a session that owns its repo already knows its own id; making it rest

- **Returns `LogSeq`** — you need a monotonic cursor, and append

- **`append_many`** — one INSERT per token-delta on the live
path won't hold up. Even if v1 doesn't batch, having

- **Cursor on `list_by
_session`** — unbounded `Vec` is fine for the mock and fatal for the fold endpoint on a long session. This is also what l

And the ordering point from before is now load-bearing rather than the
oretical: `ORDER BY created_at, id` with a random UUID tiebreak will scramble same-micro

## The manager signature has to change more than you might expect

Two independent forces:

**Postgres makes it async and fallible.** `create_session(&mut self, id: &AgentSessionId

**`&mut self -> &T` won
't survive concurrency.** Your own note on `AgentSessionRepo` says callers drive sessions from spawned tasks. A retur
ned `&T` borrows the manager for the reference's whole life, so no second task can tou

ch it. That wants `&self` + interior mutability, handing out `Arc<T>`.

Worth being explicit about the split: **
postgres owns session identity and the log; memory owns the live transport.** A live container conn

of currently-attached connections. Restart = rows survive, connections don't. That's also
where your `AcpReady` gate from earlier lands naturally — the row exists immediately, the connection bec

## On the fold

Keep it a pure function — `fold(&[AgentSessionLog])
-> MessageChain`, no I/O, no repo. Then it's trivially testable against fixtures, you can iterate the fold logic without touching stor

ist now; just don't let it grow tendrils into the repo when it

does.

**Logging is

step became half log noise. Leaving it out is cleaner, but it's a real decision, not just cosmetics: **
the pump then owns logging**, and the pump only sees what crosses the wire. So a buffered prompt
gets logged at *flush*, not at enqueue. That answers hole #4 as "the log is an honest wire transcript" — and the
cost is that a crash while a prompt sits in the buffer loses it silently. If you want the dur

## The thing I'd flag

This
test now proves the state machine *and* the transport *and* the log wiring in one go. That's what
you asked for and it's a great smoke test — but when it fails at step 4,
it won't tell you whether the bug is in the buffering, the id correlation, or the log. I'd keep it
as the one happy-path integration test and still put the edge cases (double `
AcpReady`, send-after-disconnect, `session/load` on resume) against the bare state machine where

failures are unambiguous.

Also note step 6 asserts log-at-flush — the buffered prompt appears once
, at the end, not when enqueued. If you want the dur

prompt.text: also what is a session core? this is a new thing we haven't talked about. does it own a agent client session manager AND a container session manager?

content.text: Fair — I introduced it without defining it, and it's worth pinning down because I may have over

-built.

**`SessionCore` was my name for the pure state machine**:

the decision logic with no I/O. It owns neither manager. It owns only:

- the current `

SessionState` (Booting / Handshaking / Live / Dead)
- the pending-send buffer
- the request-id counter
- the stored `acp_session_id`

and
its methods are `(&mut self, event) -> Vec<Action>`. It can

't send, can't log, can't spawn.

The intended layering was:

| Layer | Owns | I

/O |
|---|---|---|
| `AgentSessionManager` | map of sessions, postgres repo | yes |
| `AgentSessionImpl`

| container transport, log repo, a `SessionCore` | yes |
| `SessionCore` | state, buffer, counter | none

|

So: `step()` = `recv()` from the container → `core.on_inbound(msg)` → execute the returned `Action`s against

the transport and the log.

## But look at the test you just asked for

It calls `session.send
_message()`, `session.step()`, `session.state()`. **It never mentions `SessionCore` once.** The mock container plus man
ual `step()` already gives you full control of the flow — which was the ex
act problem I invented `SessionCore` to solve (I thought we'd otherwise need to fake an ACP client to get

past `AcpReady`; the mock container does that fine).

So on your own test's
evidence, the extraction isn't currently paying for itself. The simpler shape is: `AgentSessionImpl` holds

a `Mutex<SessionState>` and does the transitions inline, no separate type.

The only thing the
extraction still buys is unambiguous failures on edge cases — a `session/
load`-on-resume or double-`AcpReady` test against a bare struct tells you ex
actly what broke, where the same test through the transport implicates three lay

ers at once.

My call: **drop `SessionCore` for now.** Put the state machine inside
`AgentSessionImpl`, keep `SessionState` as a real enum, and extract later only if the
edge-case tests get hard to read. One fewer concept, and your happy-

path test is unchanged either way.

Does that match how you were picturing it, or were
you expecting the session to actually hold a container manager?

1	//! Draft `agent-runtime.v0` message types.
2	//!
3	//! The logical protocol multiplexes two kinds of traffic over one stream:
4	//! runtime/agent lifecycle events and ACP conversation traffic. Each
5	//! direction has its own envelope - [`ToRuntimeMessage`] for Agent Service to
6	//! Agent Runtime traffic and [`ToServerMessage`] for the reverse -
7	//! discriminated by a `"type"` field. Only the wrapped ACP payload is itself
8	//! a JSON-RPC message; the outer envelope is not.
9	//!
10	//! A connection hosts exactly one agent execution, so nothing on this schema
11	//! needs an agent or agent-instance identifier: [`AcpMessage`] simply carries
12	//! the agent's raw ACP traffic.

Read the relevant code. Short answer: **the gating logic is easy (~10 lines); the cost is structural plumbing in `agent_harness`, roughly a half-day.**

## What already exists

`agent_proxy` does exactly this today — `crates/agent_proxy/src/inbound/runtime.rs:123-147` waits for `SystemEvent::AcpReady` on the event channel and only then spawns `handle_agent_connected` (which runs `initialize`/`session/new`). The comment there is even the rationale you just described. So there's a proven pattern to copy.

## What's missing in `agent_harness`

Three things block a direct copy:

1. **No initialize at all.** `AgentSessionImpl` (`domain/agent_sessions/session.rs:34-40`) is a pass-through `send`/`receive` over the transport. Nothing in the harness sends an ACP handshake yet, so "wait, then initialize" means writing the initialize half too.

2. **`create_session` is sync.** `AgentSessionManager::create_session(&mut self, &AgentSessionId) -> &T` (`manager.rs:11`) can't await. Any waiting version either makes it `async` or moves the wait behind the session.

3. **Receive is pull-based and single-consumer.** `session.receive()` reads the raw transport directly. If creation loops on `recv()` waiting for the `Event`, it swallows any `Acp` frames that arrive first, and nobody else can read concurrently. You need a demux — one loop draining the transport, routing `Event{..}` → readiness signal, `Acp(..)` → the ACP side.

## Cheapest path

Don't hand-roll the demux — `agent_runtime_protocol::domain::connection::ServerConnection::connect` (`connection/mod.rs:59`) already does it: give it the channel and a `SystemEventHandler`, get back a real `agent_client_protocol::Channel`. Your handler flips a `tokio::sync::watch<bool>` on `AcpReady`.

Then pick where the wait lives:

- **Gate inside the session** (recommended): `create_session` stays sync and returns immediately; `send()` awaits the ready watch before writing, and the pump fires initialize once on the ready edge. Callers never see the gate, tests stay synchronous-ish. ~60–80 lines.
- **Async `create_session`**: smaller diff (~30 lines) but the manager blocks on a container that may never boot, and you need a timeout + a story for a container that dies pre-ready.

One open question that decides the shape: should `send()` on a not-yet-ready session **await**, **queue** (agent_proxy durably queues, per `service.rs:138-142`), or **error**? Which do you want?

content.text:
Scoped it. `agent_proxy` isn't just a crate — it's a deployed vertical slice. Here's the full surface:

## What "delete agent_proxy" actually touches

**Rust (safe, reversible via git)**
- `crates/agent_proxy` — 19 files, 3,790 lines (929-line domain service + 1,073-line test file)
- `services/agent_proxy_service` — 168 lines, the only reverse-dep of the lib
- 2 entries in root `Cargo.toml`, plus `Cargo.lock`
- `crates/macro_service_urls/src/lib.rs:540-544` — the `wss://agent-proxy{-dev}.macro.com` runtime URL
- 3 `.sqlx/query-*.json` cache entries

**Generated / cross-language**
- `packages/sdk`: `'agent-proxy'` in the service union (`config.ts:18`), 3 base URLs, `services.ts`, `specs/agent-proxy.json` — **this is a breaking change for SDK consumers**
- `apps/web/src/lib/service-clients/service-agent-proxy/` — 39 generated files + an `orval.config.ts` entry. Good news: **zero hand-written web code imports it**, so it's a pure generated-artifact delete.

Read it all. Good news first: **`agent_session` is already shaped for this.** `AgentSessionLog { agent_session_id, user_id, content: Message }` with `Message::ToServer | ToRuntime` persisted as `direction` + `content` JSONB round-trips whole protocol envelopes losslessly. You're not designing the persistence model — it exists. What you're deciding is what it *means*.

Here's what I think the real questions are.

## 1. Is the log the source of truth, or an audit trail?

This is the fork everything else hangs off.

`agent_proxy` had `translate.rs` + `TurnAccumulator` because ACP arrives as a stream of deltas and chat needs coherent messages. If you delete the proxy, that fold has to live *somewhere* — you've moved it, not removed it. Three places it can go:

- **Client-side fold.** Log is truth, UI replays raw ACP. Cleanest server, but ACP semantics leak into the frontend and every client reimplements the fold.
- **Derived projection.** Log is truth, a projector writes a read model. Most work, best reads, and replayable when the fold logic changes.
- **In-memory fold + snapshot.** Log is the write-ahead record, live state is memory, periodic snapshot. Fast, but a restart mid-turn has to replay.

Which one do you have in mind? I'd guess you're leaning at the first, and it's defensible for a coding agent where the "chat" is really a transcript.

## 2. Volume — this is the one that'll bite

ACP `session/update` notifications stream at roughly token granularity. One `INSERT` per envelope means **thousands of rows per turn**, each with a JSONB payload, on the hot path of a live stream. `AgentSessionLogRepo::create` is one-row-at-a-time with no batching.

Do you want *literally* all ACP, or all ACP *except* streaming deltas? "Persist every request/response and every terminal notification, drop the intermediate text chunks" gets you 95% of the replay value at 1% of the rows. If you do want the deltas, this needs batched or async-buffered writes before it goes near production.

## 3. Ordering is currently broken for this use case

`agent_session_log` orders by `(created_at, id)` — and `id` is a random UUID. Two rows written in the same microsecond tie-break **randomly**, which for a token stream means scrambled output. You need a monotonic `BIGSERIAL seq` (or per-session counter) as the real order key. Small migration, but it's load-bearing the moment the log becomes the transcript.

## 4. What still reaches the channel thread?

`AgentSession` keeps `created_from_thread_id` *and* its own `thread_id`. So a comms thread still exists — meaning "no longer proxy to chat" presumably means *no chat-message proxy crate*, not *no thread output*. Someone still has to post something human-readable into that thread when the agent replies. Is that a thin projector off the log, or does the agent explicitly emit "post this to the thread" actions?

## 5. Does the log make sessions resumable?

If a container dies mid-session, can you spawn a new one and replay the log into it to reconstitute state? If **yes**, the log must be complete and exact, and that kills the filtering idea in #2. If **no** — it's a transcript, resume is the harness's problem via `acp_session_id` — you have much more freedom. This one constrains #2, so it's worth answering first.

---

My instinct: **log everything except streaming text deltas, add a `seq` column, fold client-side, treat resume as out of scope for v1.** But #5 is the question that decides it — where's your head at on resumability?

That settles it — server-side fold, log as truth, and the session auto-persists. That's a coherent design and it's the one I'd pick. Three things get sharper as a consequence.

## The black box has one hole: `user_id` attribution

`AgentSessionLog.user_id` is `Some` only when the ACP originated from a user. If persistence is a side effect of `LiveAgentSession::send`, then `send()` has to know *who* — and today it takes only a message.

So the black box can't be fully blind. Either:

```rust
async fn send(&self, from: Option<MacroUserIdStr<'static>>, message: ToRuntimeMessage) -> ...
```

or two doors — `send(msg)` for harness-originated traffic, `send_from_user(user, msg)` for user-originated. I lean at the second: the call sites genuinely are two different things (a user prompt vs. the harness's own `initialize`), and the type makes you say which. `receive()` is always `user_id: None`, so it stays clean either way.

## `create` flexibility — what I think you actually need

Four pressures on that trait, in the order they'll hurt:

```rust
pub trait AgentSessionLogRepo: Send + Sync + 'static {
    /// session_id + id are implied by the owner, not passed in
    fn append(&self, entry: NewLogEntry) -> impl Future<Output = Result<LogSeq>> + Send;

    fn append_many(&self, entries: Vec<NewLogEntry>) -> impl Future<Output = Result<LogSeq>> + Send;

    fn list_by_session(
        &self,
        agent_session_id: AgentSessionId,
        after: Option<LogSeq>,
        limit: u32,
    ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Vec<AgentSessionLog>>> + Send;
}
```

- **`NewLogEntry` instead of `AgentSessionLog`** — a session that owns its repo already knows its own id; making it restate it invites mismatch. Same reasoning as `NewAgentSession` vs `AgentSession`, which you already applied one layer up.
- **Returns `LogSeq`** — you need a monotonic cursor, and append is the natural place to mint it.
- **`append_many`** — one INSERT per token-delta on the live path won't hold up. Even if v1 doesn't batch, having the door means adding buffering later isn't a trait change.
- **Cursor on `list_by_session`** — unbounded `Vec` is fine for the mock and fatal for the fold endpoint on a long session. This is also what lets the fold be incremental instead of re-reading from zero.

And the ordering point from before is now load-bearing rather than theoretical: `ORDER BY created_at, id` with a random UUID tiebreak will scramble same-microsecond writes. `LogSeq` as `BIGSERIAL` solves the cursor and the ordering in one migration.

## The manager signature has to change more than you might expect

Two independent forces:

**Postgres makes it async and fallible.** `create_session(&mut self, id: &AgentSessionId) -> &T` → probably `create_session(&self, new: NewAgentSession) -> Result<Arc<T>>`, taking `NewAgentSession` because `AgentSessionRepo::create` mints the id and thread rather than accepting them.

**`&mut self -> &T` won't survive concurrency.** Your own note on `AgentSessionRepo` says callers drive sessions from spawned tasks. A returned `&T` borrows the manager for the reference's whole life, so no second task can touch it. That wants `&self` + interior mutability, handing out `Arc<T>`.

Worth being explicit about the split: **postgres owns session identity and the log; memory owns the live transport.** A live container connection can't be persisted, so the manager is a postgres-backed registry *plus* an in-memory map of currently-attached connections. Restart = rows survive, connections don't. That's also where your `AcpReady` gate from earlier lands naturally — the row exists immediately, the connection becomes usable later.

## On the fold

Keep it a pure function — `fold(&[AgentSessionLog]) -> MessageChain`, no I/O, no repo. Then it's trivially testable against fixtures, you can iterate the fold logic without touching storage, and re-folding after a logic change is just a re-read. Doesn't need to exist now; just don't let it grow tendrils into the repo when it does.

Good — that constraint actually decides the architecture, and it points somewhere specific.

## The testability idea, taken seriously

If tests drive everything manually, the honest move is a **sans-io core**: the state machine is a plain synchronous struct that takes events and returns actions. No async, no transport, no mocks.

```rust
enum Action {
    Send(ToRuntimeMessage),
    Log(NewLogEntry),
    SetAcpSessionId(AcpId),
}

impl SessionCore {
    fn on_inbound(&mut self, msg: ToServerMessage) -> Vec<Action>;
    fn on_send(&mut self, from: Option<UserId>, msg: ToRuntimeMessage) -> Vec<Action>;
}
```

Then a test is just:

```rust
let mut core = SessionCore::booting();
assert!(core.on_send(user, prompt).is_empty());          // buffered
let actions = core.on_inbound(acp_ready());              // -> [Send(initialize)]
let actions = core.on_inbound(initialize_response());    // -> [Send(session/new)]
let actions = core.on_inbound(session_new_response());   // -> [SetAcpSessionId, Send(prompt)]
```

The reason this matters more than "don't spawn the pump": `begin_handshake` as I sketched it does real ACP round-trips inline. Even without a pump, a test would need a fake ACP client to get past `AcpReady`. Sans-io deletes that problem — the handshake responses are just more `on_inbound` calls. The cost is that request-id correlation becomes explicit state instead of hiding inside `.await`, but that complexity is real either way; this just makes it visible.

The async pump then becomes ~15 lines that execute `Action`s, and it's the only part that isn't unit-testable.

Mostly ready — and the sans-io shape means we need **types, not mocks**. That's the payoff: if `on_inbound`/`on_send` return `Vec<Action>`, tests assert on returned values. No transport double, no log double, no async, no `ContainerMock` in the core tests at all.

Three things genuinely missing first:

1. **`AcpId` is unusable.** `domain/acp_id.rs` is `pub struct AcpId(String);` — no constructor, no accessor. Needs at least `new`/`as_str`.
2. **Request-id correlation.** To recognize the `initialize` response, the core must mint `RequestId`s and remember them. I'd have it own a monotonic counter — deterministic ids make tests exact rather than "assert something was sent."
3. **`Action`, `SessionState`, `PendingSend`** — the sketch types themselves.

Notably *not* needed yet: a log-repo mock. If `Action::Log(..)` is a returned value, the core's logging is testable without any repo existing.

## Test organization

CLAUDE.md says implementation in `foo.rs`, tests in `foo/test.rs`. The existing file is `agent_sessions/tests.rs` — plural, off-convention. Worth renaming while we're here so the new module doesn't copy the deviation.

domain/session_core.rs        // SessionCore, SessionState, Action
domain/session_core/test.rs
```

## Yes, write tests now — and write them first

Sans-io makes tests the cheapest artifact in the crate, and the test *names* are the design doc. I'd rather we agree on this list than on a paragraph of prose:

```
buffers_sends_while_booting
acp_ready_emits_initialize
acp_ready_twice_starts_one_handshake
initialize_response_emits_session_new_when_fresh
initialize_response_emits_session_load_when_resuming
session_established_flushes_pending_in_order
session_established_records_acp_session_id
sends_pass_through_once_live
logs_every_inbound_message
records_unknown_system_event_as_status
send_after_disconnect_errors
```

Two of those encode decisions we haven't actually made:

- **`initialize_response_emits_session_load_when_resuming`** — depends on your answer to whether a resumed container can really `session/load`, or whether resume means a fresh ACP session with context replayed from the log.
- **Where's the log test for outbound?** I left it off deliberately: it's the enqueue-vs-flush question. If we log at enqueue, there's a `logs_pending_send_at_enqueue` test; if at flush, the ordering assertion folds into `session_established_flushes_pending_in_order`.

Want to settle those two and then I'll write the type skeleton plus that test list as `todo!()`-bodied failing tests, so we can fill them in one at a time?

the example test sketch you will show me should involve a mock container
also what is a session core? this is a new thing we haven't talked about. does it own a agent client session manager AND a container session manager?

Fair — I introduced it without defining it, and it's worth pinning down because I may have over-built.

**`SessionCore` was my name for the pure state machine**: the decision logic with no I/O. It owns neither manager. It owns only:

- the current `SessionState` (Booting / Handshaking / Live / Dead)
- the pending-send buffer
- the request-id counter
- the stored `acp_session_id`

and its methods are `(&mut self, event) -> Vec<Action>`. It can't send, can't log, can't spawn.

The intended layering was:

| Layer | Owns | I/O |
|---|---|---|
| `AgentSessionManager` | map of sessions, postgres repo | yes |
| `AgentSessionImpl` | container transport, log repo, a `SessionCore` | yes |
| `SessionCore` | state, buffer, counter | none |

So: `step()` = `recv()` from the container → `core.on_inbound(msg)` → execute the returned `Action`s against the transport and the log.

## But look at the test you just asked for

It calls `session.send_message()`, `session.step()`, `session.state()`. **It never mentions `SessionCore` once.** The mock container plus manual `step()` already gives you full control of the flow — which was the exact problem I invented `SessionCore` to solve (I thought we'd otherwise need to fake an ACP client to get past `AcpReady`; the mock container does that fine).

So on your own test's evidence, the extraction isn't currently paying for itself. The simpler shape is: `AgentSessionImpl` holds a `Mutex<SessionState>` and does the transitions inline, no separate type.

The only thing the extraction still buys is unambiguous failures on edge cases — a `session/load`-on-resume or double-`AcpReady` test against a bare struct tells you exactly what broke, where the same test through the transport implicates three layers at once.

My call: **drop `SessionCore` for now.** Put the state machine inside `AgentSessionImpl`, keep `SessionState` as a real enum, and extract later only if the edge-case tests get hard to read. One fewer concept, and your happy-path test is unchanged either way.

1	//! Draft `agent-runtime.v0` message types.
2	//!
3	//! The logical protocol multiplexes two kinds of traffic over one stream:
4	//! runtime/agent lifecycle events and ACP conversation traffic. Each
5	//! direction has its own envelope - [`ToRuntimeMessage`] for Agent Service to
6	//! Agent Runtime traffic and [`ToServerMessage`] for the reverse -
7	//! discriminated by a `"type"` field. Only the wrapped ACP payload is itself
8	//! a JSON-RPC message; the outer envelope is not.
9	//!
10	//! A connection hosts exactly one agent execution, so nothing on this schema
11	//! needs an agent or agent-instance identifier: [`AcpMessage`] simply carries
12	//! the agent's raw ACP traffic.
13	
14	use agent_client_protocol::RawJsonRpcMessage;
15	use serde::{Deserialize, Deserializer, Serialize, Serializer};
16	use specta::Type;
17	use specta_typescript::Unknown;
18	
19	#[cfg(test)]
20	mod test;
21	
22	/// The kind of runtime or agent state transition reported to the Agent Service.
23	///
24	/// The protocol does not define a full event-name catalog yet, so this enum
25	/// is non-exhaustive: unrecognized wire strings still round-trip losslessly
26	/// through [`SystemEvent::Unknown`]. [`SystemEvent::AcpReady`] is the one
27	/// name the Agent Service actually acts on (see
28	/// `agent_proxy::inbound::runtime::RuntimeConnectionDriver`, which waits for
29	/// it before starting the ACP `initialize`/`session/new` handshake) rather
30	/// than merely forwarding it for observability.
31	///
32	/// This has a hand-written [`Serialize`]/[`Deserialize`] impl rather than a
33	/// derive, so it cannot derive [`specta::Type`] either: nothing here
34	/// introspects its shape for TypeScript. Every field that carries a
35	/// `SystemEvent` is instead given a `#[specta(type = String)]` override at
36	/// the field, matching the plain string it actually serializes as.
37	#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq, Hash)]
38	#[non_exhaustive]
39	pub enum SystemEvent {
40	    /// The Agent Runtime's hosted agent process is up and its ACP channel is
41	    /// wired end-to-end: the Agent Service may now start the ACP
42	    /// `initialize`/`session/new` handshake. Sent at most once per
43	    /// connection, before any ACP traffic.
44	    AcpReady,
45	    /// An application-defined event name with no protocol-level meaning yet.
46	    Unknown(String),
47	}
48	
49	impl SystemEvent {
50	    /// Borrow the wire string for this event name.
51	    #[must_use]
52	    pub fn as_str(&self) -> &str {
53	        match self {
54	            Self::AcpReady => "acp_ready",
55	            Self::Unknown(name) => name,
56	        }
57	    }
58	}
59	
60	impl Serialize for SystemEvent {
61	    fn serialize<S>(&self, serializer: S) -> Result<S::Ok, S::Error>
62	    where
63	        S: Serializer,
64	    {
65	        serializer.serialize_str(self.as_str())
66	    }
67	}
68	
69	impl<'de> Deserialize<'de> for SystemEvent {
70	    fn deserialize<D>(deserializer: D) -> Result<Self, D::Error>
71	    where
72	        D: Deserializer<'de>,
73	    {
74	        Ok(match String::deserialize(deserializer)?.as_str() {
75	            "acp_ready" => Self::AcpReady,
76	            name => Self::Unknown(name.to_owned()),
77	        })
78	    }
79	}
80	
81	/// One complete ACP JSON-RPC message routed between the Agent Service and the
82	/// single agent execution hosted by this connection.
83	///
84	/// Its own JSON-RPC fields are opaque to TypeScript consumers here (typed as
85	/// an arbitrary object of unknown values): they already have a proper ACP SDK
86	/// on the TypeScript side, so this crate only needs to guarantee the message
87	/// round-trips unchanged. This is typed as a map rather than plain `unknown`
88	/// because [`ToRuntimeMessage`]/[`ToServerMessage`] carry it in an internally
89	/// tagged `Acp` variant, which requires its payload provably serialize as an
90	/// object so the `"type"` tag can be merged into it. `#[serde(transparent)]`
91	/// changes nothing about the actual wire format here - a single-field tuple
92	/// struct already serializes transparently by default - but it does tell
93	/// specta's serde-compatibility checker that this newtype is transparent, so
94	/// it looks through to the map type below instead of treating `AcpMessage`
95	/// itself as an opaque, non-mergeable struct.
96	#[derive(Debug, Clone, Serialize, Deserialize, Type)]
97	#[serde(transparent)]
98	pub struct AcpMessage(
99	    #[specta(type = std::collections::HashMap<String, Unknown>)] pub RawJsonRpcMessage,
100	);
101	
102	/// Agent Service to Agent Runtime traffic on the logical protocol stream.
103	#[derive(Debug, Clone, Serialize, Deserialize, Type)]
104	#[serde(tag = "type", rename_all = "camelCase")]
105	#[non_exhaustive]
106	pub enum ToRuntimeMessage {
107	    /// An ACP message routed to the hosted agent.
108	    Acp(AcpMessage),
109	}
110	
111	/// Agent Runtime to Agent Service traffic on the logical protocol stream.
112	#[derive(Debug, Clone, Serialize, Deserialize, Type)]
113	#[serde(tag = "type", rename_all = "camelCase")]
114	#[non_exhaustive]
115	pub enum ToServerMessage {
116	    /// An ACP message routed from the hosted agent.
117	    Acp(AcpMessage),
118	    /// A runtime or agent lifecycle event.
119	    Event {
120	        /// The event name.
121	        #[specta(type = String)]
122	        event: SystemEvent,
123	    },
124	}

Read the relevant code. Short answer: **the gating logic is easy (~10 lines); the cost is structural plumbing in `agent_harness`, roughly a half-day.**

## What already exists

`agent_proxy` does exactly this today — `crates/agent_proxy/src/inbound/runtime.rs:123-147` waits for `SystemEvent::AcpReady` on the event channel and only then spawns `handle_agent_connected` (which runs `initialize`/`session/new`). The comment there is even the rationale you just described. So there's a proven pattern to copy.

## What's missing in `agent_harness`

Three things block a direct copy:

1. **No initialize at all.** `AgentSessionImpl` (`domain/agent_sessions/session.rs:34-40`) is a pass-through `send`/`receive` over the transport. Nothing in the harness sends an ACP handshake yet, so "wait, then initialize" means writing the initialize half too.

2. **`create_session` is sync.** `AgentSessionManager::create_session(&mut self, &AgentSessionId) -> &T` (`manager.rs:11`) can't await. Any waiting version either makes it `async` or moves the wait behind the session.

3. **Receive is pull-based and single-consumer.** `session.receive()` reads the raw transport directly. If creation loops on `recv()` waiting for the `Event`, it swallows any `Acp` frames that arrive first, and nobody else can read concurrently. You need a demux — one loop draining the transport, routing `Event{..}` → readiness signal, `Acp(..)` → the ACP side.

## Cheapest path

Don't hand-roll the demux — `agent_runtime_protocol::domain::connection::ServerConnection::connect` (`connection/mod.rs:59`) already does it: give it the channel and a `SystemEventHandler`, get back a real `agent_client_protocol::Channel`. Your handler flips a `tokio::sync::watch<bool>` on `AcpReady`.

Then pick where the wait lives:

- **Gate inside the session** (recommended): `create_session` stays sync and returns immediately; `send()` awaits the ready watch before writing, and the pump fires initialize once on the ready edge. Callers never see the gate, tests stay synchronous-ish. ~60–80 lines.
- **Async `create_session`**: smaller diff (~30 lines) but the manager blocks on a container that may never boot, and you need a timeout + a story for a container that dies pre-ready.

One open question that decides the shape: should `send()` on a not-yet-ready session **await**, **queue** (agent_proxy durably queues, per `service.rs:138-142`), or **error**? Which do you want?

Scoped it. `agent_proxy` isn't just a crate — it's a deployed vertical slice. Here's the full surface:

## What "delete agent_proxy" actually touches

**Rust (safe, reversible via git)**
- `crates/agent_proxy` — 19 files, 3,790 lines (929-line domain service + 1,073-line test file)
- `services/agent_proxy_service` — 168 lines, the only reverse-dep of the lib
- 2 entries in root `Cargo.toml`, plus `Cargo.lock`
- `crates/macro_service_urls/src/lib.rs:540-544` — the `wss://agent-proxy{-dev}.macro.com` runtime URL
- 3 `.sqlx/query-*.json` cache entries

**Generated / cross-language**
- `packages/sdk`: `'agent-proxy'` in the service union (`config.ts:18`), 3 base URLs, `services.ts`, `specs/agent-proxy.json` — **this is a breaking change for SDK consumers**
- `apps/web/src/lib/service-clients/service-agent-proxy/` — 39 generated files + an `orval.config.ts` entry. Good news: **zero hand-written web code imports it**, so it's a pure generated-artifact delete.
- `.github/workspace-dep-closures.json`, `docker/docker-compose.yml`, `docker/Dockerfile.dev`, `infra/local/generated/acp/*`

**Deployed state — I won't touch this without an explicit go**
- `infra/stacks/agent-proxy-service/` has `Pulumi.dev.yaml` **and `Pulumi.prod.yaml`** — there's a live prod service. Deleting the stack source orphans real cloud resources; they need `pulumi destroy` first, by you.
- `infra/stacks/doppler-projects/index.ts` has an agent-proxy project.
- `crates/macro_db_client/migrations/20260729215917_agent_proxy_pending_messages.sql` — **already applied**. Deleting an applied migration breaks every environment's migration ledger. The right move is a new `DROP TABLE` migration, not a file delete.

## Two things worth deciding before I start

1. **`agent_harness` is not close to parity.** Its whole domain is ~200 lines of session/container scaffolding. `agent_proxy` carries the ACP handshake, the `AcpReady` gate you just asked about, the pending-message queue, turn accumulation, chat persistence, and 5 HTTP routes (`/agents`, `/sessions/{id}/acp`, `/runtime` WS upgrade). Deleting it now also deletes the reference implementation for the feature in your previous message. Only doc comments in `agent_harness` reference it — no code coupling — so it can stay around harmlessly while you port.

2. **Scope.** Which do you want?
   - **(a) Full teardown now** — everything above except infra-destroy and the migration, which I'd stage as a drop-migration and a written handoff for you to run.
   - **(b) Code-only** — delete the crate + service + Cargo/SDK/web wiring, leave `infra/` and the migration entirely alone for a later pass.
   - **(c) Port first** — I lift the `AcpReady` gate and handshake into `agent_harness`, get it working, *then* we delete.

My read is **(c) then (a)** — but if `agent_harness_service` is already the intended replacement and you just want the dead weight gone, (b) is a clean single commit. Which way?

content.text:
Read it all. Good news first: **`agent_session` is already shaped for this.** `AgentSessionLog { agent_session_id, user_id, content: Message }` with `Message::ToServer | ToRuntime` persisted as `direction` + `content` JSONB round-trips whole protocol envelopes losslessly. You're not designing the persistence model — it exists. What you're deciding is what it *means*.

Here's what I think the real questions are.

## 1. Is the log the source of truth, or an audit trail?

This is the fork everything else hangs off.

`agent_proxy` had `translate.rs` + `TurnAccumulator` because ACP arrives as a stream of deltas and chat needs coherent messages. If you delete the proxy, that fold has to live *somewhere* — you've moved it, not removed it. Three places it can go:

- **Client-side fold.** Log is truth, UI replays raw ACP. Cleanest server, but ACP semantics leak into the frontend and every client reimplements the fold.
- **Derived projection.** Log is truth, a projector writes a read model. Most work, best reads, and replayable when the fold logic changes.
- **In-memory fold + snapshot.** Log is the write-ahead record, live state is memory, periodic snapshot. Fast, but a restart mid-turn has to replay.

Which one do you have in mind? I'd guess you're leaning at the first, and it's defensible for a coding agent where the "chat" is really a transcript.

## 2. Volume — this is the one that'll bite

ACP `session/update` notifications stream at roughly token granularity. One `INSERT` per envelope means **thousands of rows per turn**, each with a JSONB payload, on the hot path of a live stream. `AgentSessionLogRepo::create` is one-row-at-a-time with no batching.

Do you want *literally* all ACP, or all ACP *except* streaming deltas? "Persist every request/response and every terminal notification, drop the intermediate text chunks" gets you 95% of the replay value at 1% of the rows. If you do want the deltas, this needs batched or async-buffered writes before it goes near production.

## 3. Ordering is currently broken for this use case

`agent_session_log` orders by `(created_at, id)` — and `id` is a random UUID. Two rows written in the same microsecond tie-break **randomly**, which for a token stream means scrambled output. You need a monotonic `BIGSERIAL seq` (or per-session counter) as the real order key. Small migration, but it's load-bearing the moment the log becomes the transcript.

## 4. What still reaches the channel thread?

`AgentSession` keeps `created_from_thread_id` *and* its own `thread_id`. So a comms thread still exists — meaning "no longer proxy to chat" presumably means *no chat-message proxy crate*, not *no thread output*. Someone still has to post something human-readable into that thread when the agent replies. Is that a thin projector off the log, or does the agent explicitly emit "post this to the thread" actions?

## 5. Does the log make sessions resumable?

If a container dies mid-session, can you spawn a new one and replay the log into it to reconstitute state? If **yes**, the log must be complete and exact, and that kills the filtering idea in #2. If **no** — it's a transcript, resume is the harness's problem via `acp_session_id` — you have much more freedom. This one constrains #2, so it's worth answering first.

---

My instinct: **log everything except streaming text deltas, add a `seq` column, fold client-side, treat resume as out of scope for v1.** But #5 is the question that decides it — where's your head at on resumability?

pub trait AgentSessionLogRepo: Send + Sync + 'static {
    /// Append a new log entry to a session's history.
    fn create(&self, log: AgentSessionLog) -> impl Future<Output = Result<()>> + Send;

    /// List all log entries for a session, in chronological order.

        agent_session_id: AgentSessionId,

</context>

That settles it — server-side fold, log as truth, and the session auto-persists. That's a coherent design and it's the one I'd pick. Three things get sharper as a consequence.

## The black box has one hole: `user_id` attribution

`AgentSessionLog.user_id` is `Some` only when the ACP originated from a user. If persistence is a side effect of `LiveAgentSession::send`, then `send()` has to know *who* — and today it takes only a message.

So the black box can't be fully blind. Either:

```rust
async fn send(&self, from: Option<MacroUserIdStr<'static>>, message: ToRuntimeMessage) -> ...
```

or two doors — `send(msg)` for harness-originated traffic, `send_from_user(user, msg)` for user-originated. I lean at the second: the call sites genuinely are two different things (a user prompt vs. the harness's own `initialize`), and the type makes you say which. `receive()` is always `user_id: None`, so it stays clean either way.

## `create` flexibility — what I think you actually need

Four pressures on that trait, in the order they'll hurt:

```rust
pub trait AgentSessionLogRepo: Send + Sync + 'static {
    /// session_id + id are implied by the owner, not passed in
    fn append(&self, entry: NewLogEntry) -> impl Future<Output = Result<LogSeq>> + Send;

    fn append_many(&self, entries: Vec<NewLogEntry>) -> impl Future<Output = Result<LogSeq>> + Send;

    fn list_by_session(
        &self,
        agent_session_id: AgentSessionId,
        after: Option<LogSeq>,
        limit: u32,
    ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Vec<AgentSessionLog>>> + Send;
}
```

- **`NewLogEntry` instead of `AgentSessionLog`** — a session that owns its repo already knows its own id; making it restate it invites mismatch. Same reasoning as `NewAgentSession` vs `AgentSession`, which you already applied one layer up.
- **Returns `LogSeq`** — you need a monotonic cursor, and append is the natural place to mint it.
- **`append_many`** — one INSERT per token-delta on the live path won't hold up. Even if v1 doesn't batch, having the door means adding buffering later isn't a trait change.
- **Cursor on `list_by_session`** — unbounded `Vec` is fine for the mock and fatal for the fold endpoint on a long session. This is also what lets the fold be incremental instead of re-reading from zero.

And the ordering point from before is now load-bearing rather than theoretical: `ORDER BY created_at, id` with a random UUID tiebreak will scramble same-microsecond writes. `LogSeq` as `BIGSERIAL` solves the cursor and the ordering in one migration.

## The manager signature has to change more than you might expect

Two independent forces:

**Postgres makes it async and fallible.** `create_session(&mut self, id: &AgentSessionId) -> &T` → probably `create_session(&self, new: NewAgentSession) -> Result<Arc<T>>`, taking `NewAgentSession` because `AgentSessionRepo::create` mints the id and thread rather than accepting them.

**`&mut self -> &T` won't survive concurrency.** Your own note on `AgentSessionRepo` says callers drive sessions from spawned tasks. A returned `&T` borrows the manager for the reference's whole life, so no second task can touch it. That wants `&self` + interior mutability, handing out `Arc<T>`.

Worth being explicit about the split: **postgres owns session identity and the log; memory owns the live transport.** A live container connection can't be persisted, so the manager is a postgres-backed registry *plus* an in-memory map of currently-attached connections. Restart = rows survive, connections don't. That's also where your `AcpReady` gate from earlier lands naturally — the row exists immediately, the connection becomes usable later.

## On the fold

Keep it a pure function — `fold(&[AgentSessionLog]) -> MessageChain`, no I/O, no repo. Then it's trivially testable against fixtures, you can iterate the fold logic without touching storage, and re-folding after a logic change is just a re-read. Doesn't need to exist now; just don't let it grow tendrils into the repo when it does.

---

Good — that constraint actually decides the architecture, and it points somewhere specific.

## The testability idea, taken seriously

If tests drive everything manually, the honest move is a **sans-io core**: the state machine is a plain synchronous struct that takes events and returns actions. No async, no transport, no mocks.

```rust
enum Action {
    Send(ToRuntimeMessage),
    Log(NewLogEntry),
    SetAcpSessionId(AcpId),
}

impl SessionCore {
    fn on_inbound(&mut self, msg: ToServerMessage) -> Vec<Action>;
    fn on_send(&mut self, from: Option<UserId>, msg: ToRuntimeMessage) -> Vec<Action>;
}
```

Then a test is just:

```rust
let mut core = SessionCore::booting();
assert!(core.on_send(user, prompt).is_empty());          // buffered
let actions = core.on_inbound(acp_ready());              // -> [Send(initialize)]
let actions = core.on_inbound(initialize_response());    // -> [Send(session/new)]
let actions = core.on_inbound(session_new_response());   // -> [SetAcpSessionId, Send(prompt)]
```

The reason this matters more than "don't spawn the pump": `begin_handshake` as I sketched it does real ACP round-trips inline. Even without a pump, a test would need a fake ACP client to get past `AcpReady`. Sans-io deletes that problem — the handshake responses are just more `on_inbound` calls. The cost is that request-id correlation becomes explicit state instead of hiding inside `.await`, but that complexity is real either way; this just makes it visible.

The async pump then becomes ~15 lines that execute `Action`s, and it's the only part that isn't unit-testable.

**But it forks the handshake.** `AgentSession.acp_session_id: Option<String>` exists exactly for this, and now I see why:

- `NewSession` → `acp_session_id` is `None` → `initialize` then **`session/new`**
- `ChannelEvent` resume → `acp_session_id` is `Some` → `initialize` then **`session/load`**

So `Handshaking` branches on the stored id. Worth building that in from the start rather than retrofitting — it's one match arm now and a surgery later. Does the container actually preserve enough state for `session/load` to work after a sandbox restart, or does resume in practice mean "new ACP session, replay context from the log"? That changes which one we call.

**One gap left.** `NewSession` carries three thread ids and no `message_id`. But the message that triggered it was posted *before* the session existed, so it can't arrive as a `ChannelEvent` either. So on `NewSession` we must go read the thread ourselves to build the first prompt — meaning a "read thread contents" outbound port, and `sub_thread_id`/`top_level_thread_id` are what we read. Is that right, or does the first prompt reach us some other way?

//! Bridge a sidecar WebSocket to typed ACP frames.
//!
//! Shared by both providers: Daytona dials the sidecar through a preview URL
//! and Namespace through an ingress, but past the dial the protocol is
//! identical, so the pump is written once here.
//!
//! ## One message, one frame
//!
//! There is no buffering, splitting, or partial-line handling, because the
//! sidecar does not stream bytes. `container/sidecar` reads the agent's stdout
//! with `BufReader::lines()` and sends each complete line as one WebSocket
//! text message; WebSocket is message-oriented and tungstenite reassembles
//! fragmented frames before yielding a `Message`. So every message that
//! arrives is exactly one JSON value.
//!
//! The same holds outbound, with one wrinkle worth not re-learning: the
//! sidecar appends the newline to the agent's stdin itself, so frames are sent
//! *without* a trailing newline. Adding one here puts a blank line into the
//! agent's stdin after every frame.
//!
//! If the sidecar ever becomes a genuine byte pipe, this is where the framing
//! would come back - and at that point `tokio_util::codec` over
//! `ws_stream_tungstenite` is a better answer than a hand-rolled buffer.

use agent_client_protocol::RawJsonRpcMessage;
use agent_runtime_protocol::domain::channel::Channel;
use futures::{SinkExt, StreamExt};
use tokio::io::{AsyncRead, AsyncWrite};
use tokio_tungstenite::WebSocketStream;
use tokio_tungstenite::tungstenite::Message;

use crate::domain::ports::AcpFrames;

/// Wire a connected sidecar socket to a channel of typed ACP frames.
///
/// Returns the caller's end; the pump runs on its own task until either side
/// closes.
pub fn spawn<Socket>(socket: WebSocketStream<Socket>) -> AcpFrames
where
    Socket: AsyncRead + AsyncWrite + Unpin + Send + 'static,
{
    let (ours, theirs) = Channel::duplex();
    tokio::spawn(pump(socket, theirs));
    ours
}

/// Relay frames until either side closes.
async fn pump<Socket>(
    socket: WebSocketStream<Socket>,
    side: Channel<RawJsonRpcMessage, RawJsonRpcMessage>,
) where
    Socket: AsyncRead + AsyncWrite + Unpin + Send + 'static,
{
    let (mut socket_tx, mut socket_rx) = socket.split();
    let Channel { tx, mut rx } = side;

    loop {
        tokio::select! {
            outbound = rx.recv() => {
                let Some(frame) = outbound else { break };
                // A frame we just built failing to serialize is not worth
                // tearing the session down over.
                let Ok(json) = serde_json::to_string(&frame) else {
                    tracing::error!("could not serialize an outgoing acp frame");
                    continue;
                };
                if socket_tx.send(Message::Text(json.into())).await.is_err() {
                    break;
                }
            }
            inbound = socket_rx.next() => {
                let json = match inbound {
                    Some(Ok(Message::Text(text))) => text.to_string(),
                    Some(Ok(Message::Binary(data))) => match String::from_utf8(data.to_vec()) {
                        Ok(text) => text,
                        Err(error) => {
                            tracing::error!(?error, "agent sent a non-utf8 acp frame");
                            continue;
                        }
                    },
                    // Not part of the protocol.
                    Some(Ok(Message::Ping(_) | Message::Pong(_) | Message::Frame(_))) => continue,
                    Some(Ok(Message::Close(_)) | Err(_)) | None => break,
                };

                match serde_json::from_str::<RawJsonRpcMessage>(&json) {
                    Ok(frame) => {
                        if tx.send(frame).is_err() {
                            break;
                        }
                    }
                    // One unparseable frame is not fatal: the agent keeps
                    // talking, and dropping the session would lose the rest.
                    Err(error) => {
                        tracing::error!(?error, %json, "agent sent an unparseable acp frame");
                    }
                }
            }
        }
    }
    tracing::debug!("sidecar pump finished");
}

options.name: honeycomb:honeycomb-investigator
options.description:
Use this agent when the user needs an autonomous, multi-step investigation of a production
issue using Honeycomb. Examples:

<example>
Context: User received a PagerDuty alert about high latency
user: "Our checkout API is slow, can you investigate using Honeycomb?"
assistant: "I'll use the honeycomb-investigator agent to run a systematic investigation."
<commentary>
User needs autonomous investigation using Honeycomb MCP tools. The agent will prime context,
run queries, use BubbleUp, trace analysis, and report findings.
</commentary>
</example>

<example>
Context: User sees errors in production after a deployment
user: "We deployed v2.5 and errors spiked. Investigate what went wrong in Honeycomb."
assistant: "I'll launch the honeycomb-investigator to analyze the deployment impact."
<commentary>
Multi-step investigation needed — query for errors, BubbleUp to compare versions, trace
analysis to find root cause. Agent orchestrates the full workflow.
</commentary>
</example>

<example>
Context: SLO budget is burning fast
user: "Our checkout SLO is burning budget fast. Can you figure out what's going on?"
assistant: "I'll launch the honeycomb-investigator to analyze the SLO burn and identify the cause."
<commentary>
SLO-driven investigation. Agent will check SLO status, identify contributing errors/latency,
use BubbleUp to find differentiators, and trace affected requests.
</commentary>
</example>

options.name: honeycomb:instrumentation-advisor
options.description:
Use this agent when the user wants to improve their application's observability by analyzing
their codebase against what Honeycomb actually receives. This agent autonomously scans code,
queries Honeycomb for existing coverage, and produces a prioritized gap analysis with
ready-to-apply code. Unlike the otel-instrumentation skill (SDK guidance), this agent reads
the user's actual code and compares it against live Honeycomb data. Examples:

<example>
Context: User wants to know what they should instrument next
user: "What's missing from our instrumentation? We have basic tracing but I feel like we're not getting enough detail."
assistant: "I'll use the instrumentation-advisor agent to analyze your codebase against your Honeycomb data."
<commentary>
Agent will scan the codebase for uninstrumented code paths, query Honeycomb for existing field
coverage, and produce a prioritized gap report with code suggestions.
</commentary>
</example>

<example>
Context: User wants to add observability to a specific service
user: "Can you instrument our checkout service? It's in Go and we have basic OTel but no custom spans."
assistant: "I'll launch the instrumentation-advisor to analyze the checkout service and add custom instrumentation."
<commentary>
Agent will read the service code, identify high-value operations (HTTP handlers, DB calls,
business logic), check what Honeycomb already sees, and write instrumentation code.
</commentary>
</example>

<example>
Context: User is debugging and notices gaps in their traces
user: "Our traces are missing context — I can't tell which user or tenant is affected. Can you fix that?"
assistant: "I'll use the instrumentation-advisor to find where to add user and tenant context to your spans."
<commentary>
Attribute enrichment task. Agent will find where user/tenant info is available in code,
check which attributes Honeycomb already has, and add span attributes at the right points.
</commentary>
</example>

availableCommands.name: honeycomb:metrics-queries
availableCommands.description: (honeycomb) How to query OpenTelemetry metrics datasets in Honeycomb correctly. Metrics datasets follow different rules from trace/event datasets — many operations (bare COUNT, RATE_SUM, RATE_AVG, RATE_MAX, CONCURRENCY) are forbidden, temporal aggregation is automatic, and each metric has its own attributes. Use this skill when querying a metrics dataset (gauges, counters, histograms, sums), asking about temporal aggregation (RATE, INCREASE, SUMMARIZE, LAST), finding the metrics dataset or discovering metric names and attributes, debugging unexpected metrics query results, or querying infrastructure metrics like CPU, memory, disk I/O, or network stats. Do NOT use for instrumenting metrics (use otel-instrumentation), querying event datasets with "metrics" in their name, or conceptual questions (use observability-fundamentals).

availableCommands.name: honeycomb:observability-fundamentals
availableCommands.description: (honeycomb) First principles behind observability — wide events, high cardinality, the core analysis loop, events vs metrics vs logs, and how instrumentation connects to debugging outcomes. Grounds recommendations in first principles rather than tool-specific how-to. Trigger phrases: "what is observability", "why observability", "why Honeycomb", "events vs metrics vs logs", "events vs metrics", "events vs logs", "metrics vs logs", "why wide events", "what is high cardinality", "core analysis loop", "observability vs monitoring", "what is dimensionality", "explain observability", or any conceptual question about observability or why Honeycomb's approach differs from traditional monitoring.

availableCommands.name: honeycomb:otel-genai-instrumentation
availableCommands.description: (honeycomb) Guides instrumentation of GenAI/LLM applications with OpenTelemetry for Honeycomb, including content capture and agent failure detection. Trigger phrases: "instrument my GenAI app", "add tracing to LLM calls", "trace AI agent", "instrument OpenAI", "instrument Anthropic", "GenAI observability", "trace tool calling", "LLM token usage", "instrument embeddings", "trace MCP", "GenAI metrics", "instrument LangChain", "add GenAI spans", "capture prompts", "capture LLM responses", "enable GenAI content capture", "streaming tracing", "trace streaming responses", or any request about instrumenting GenAI/LLM applications.

availableCommands.name: honeycomb:otel-instrumentation
availableCommands.description: (honeycomb) Provides guidance on OpenTelemetry SDK setup, custom instrumentation, and sending data to Honeycomb. Trigger phrases: "instrument my app", "add tracing", "set up OpenTelemetry", "configure OTel", "add custom spans", "add attributes to spans", "send traces to Honeycomb", "set up OTLP", "configure sampling", "add span events", "add span links", "set up tracing for [any language]", "configure the OTel Collector", or any request about OpenTelemetry SDK setup, custom instrumentation, or sending data to Honeycomb.

availableCommands.name: honeycomb:otel-migration
availableCommands.description: (honeycomb) Guide for retrofitting OpenTelemetry into an existing, uninstrumented application. Trigger phrases: "migrate existing app to OTel", "add OpenTelemetry to existing project", "retrofit OTel into my codebase", "thread context through my code", "context propagation", "bridge Prometheus metrics to OTel", "logging bridge", "migrate logging to OTel", "slog bridge", "logback bridge", "verify my instrumentation", "traces are disconnected", "orphaned spans", "migrate to OpenTelemetry", "OTel migration plan", "how do I sequence an OTel migration", "add tracing to existing code", "refactor for context propagation", "Fiber context gotcha", "keep existing logging working with OTel", "add OTel without breaking Prometheus", "bridge existing metrics", "coexist with existing monitoring", or any request about retrofitting OpenTelemetry into an existing application. This skill is for migrating existing codebases, NOT greenfield instrumentation (use otel-instrumentation) or Beeline-specific migration (use beeline-migration).

availableCommands.name: honeycomb:production-investigation
availableCommands.description: (honeycomb) Structured workflows for investigating production issues in Honeycomb — the sequence of tool calls (context priming, broad query, BubbleUp, trace analysis, verification) and how to chain results between steps to reach root causes. Trigger phrases: "investigate production issue", "debug latency spike", "find root cause", "use BubbleUp", "analyze traces", "debug an outage", "why is my API slow", "errors are increasing", "health check", "SLO burning", or any request to investigate or debug production problems.

availableCommands.name: honeycomb:query-patterns
availableCommands.description: (honeycomb) Opinionated guidance for constructing and interpreting Honeycomb queries on trace and event datasets — operation selection (percentiles not AVG, HEATMAP for distributions), relational field patterns (root., parent., any., none.), calculated fields, query math, and result interpretation (P99/P50 ratios, heatmap bands, TOTAL/OTHER rows, raw JSON via query_result_json). Use this skill when the user wants to query spans, traces, or log/event data in Honeycomb — requests like "show me latency", "error rate", "find slow requests", "find outliers", "interpret results", "relational fields", "calculated fields", or "download raw results". This skill covers all dataset types except metrics datasets (dataset_type=metrics) — for those, use metrics-queries instead.

availableCommands.name: honeycomb:slos-and-triggers
availableCommands.description: (honeycomb) Decision heuristics for interpreting Honeycomb SLO compliance, budget burn rates, and trigger status — what the numbers mean and what action to take, including detecting misconfigured SLIs, deciding when to freeze deploys vs page on-call, and designing burn alert thresholds. Load this skill before calling get_slos or get_triggers. Trigger phrases: "check our SLOs", "are we meeting our SLOs", "which SLOs are healthy", "is the error budget OK", "are any alerts firing", "what's the burn rate", "set up an SLO", "create a trigger", "configure alerts", "set up burn alerts", "check trigger status", "starting on-call", "reliability picture", "should we freeze deploys", "is this SLO misconfigured", "are we within budget", "SLO is broken", "budget is negative", or any request about service level objectives, error budgets, burn rates, or alerting in Honeycomb.

availableCommands.name: honeycomb:verify-recent-trace
