availableCommands.name: design-sync
availableCommands.description: Push a React design system to claude.ai/design. This runs a converter that bundles the real component code (from Storybook or a bare package) and uploads it. Use when the user runs /design-sync or says "sync my design system to Claude Design".

availableCommands.name: dataviz
availableCommands.description: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".

availableCommands.name: update-config
availableCommands.description: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.

availableCommands.name: verify
availableCommands.description: Verify that a code change actually does what it's supposed to by exercising it end-to-end and observing behavior — drive the affected flow, not just tests or typecheck. Run before committing nontrivial changes; bootstraps this repo's project verify skill if none exists yet. Don't invoke it on a diff that only touches tests, docs, or other code with no runtime surface to drive (a change to product source always has one) — there's nothing to observe.

availableCommands.name: doctor
availableCommands.description: Health-check the user's Claude Code setup and fix issues: diagnose installation health — what the `claude doctor` terminal diagnostics cover — from local data (duplicate or leftover installs, PATH, unparseable settings files, broken or colliding agent definitions); find unused skills, MCP servers, and plugins versus their context cost and disable dead weight; deduplicate local CLAUDE.md files against checked-in ones; trim checked-in CLAUDE.md files by cutting content a session could derive from the codebase (directory layouts, tech-stack lists, architecture overviews) while keeping gotchas, rationale, and non-standard conventions; migrate always-loaded CLAUDE.md guidance into lazy skills and nested CLAUDE.md files; flag slow hooks and context-heavy extensions; check the installed version is current; make auto mode the default permission mode; and pre-approve frequently denied read-only commands. Use when the user asks for a doctor run, checkup, audit, tune-up, or cleanup of their Claude Code setup or configuration.

availableCommands.name: loop

availableCommands.name: claude-api
availableCommands.description:
Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).

1	//! Draft `agent-runtime.v0` message types.
2	//!
3	//! The logical protocol multiplexes two kinds of traffic over one stream:
4	//! runtime/agent lifecycle events and ACP conversation traffic. Each
5	//! direction has its own envelope - [`ToRuntimeMessage`] for Agent Service to
6	//! Agent Runtime traffic and [`ToServerMessage`] for the reverse -
7	//! discriminated by a `"type"` field. Only the wrapped ACP payload is itself
8	//! a JSON-RPC message; the outer envelope is not.
9	//!
10	//! A connection hosts exactly one agent execution, so nothing on this schema
11	//! needs an agent or agent-instance identifier: [`AcpMessage`] simply carries
12	//! the agent's raw ACP traffic.
13	
14	use agent_client_protocol::RawJsonRpcMessage;
15	use serde::{Deserialize, Deserializer, Serialize, Serializer};
16	use specta::Type;
17	use specta_typescript::Unknown;
18	
19	#[cfg(test)]
20	mod test;
21	
22	/// The kind of runtime or agent state transition reported to the Agent Service.
23	///
24	/// The protocol does not define a full event-name catalog yet, so this enum
25	/// is non-exhaustive: unrecognized wire strings still round-trip losslessly
26	/// through [`SystemEvent::Unknown`]. [`SystemEvent::AcpReady`] is the one
27	/// name the Agent Service actually acts on (see
28	/// `agent_proxy::inbound::runtime::RuntimeConnectionDriver`, which waits for
29	/// it before starting the ACP `initialize`/`session/new` handshake) rather
30	/// than merely forwarding it for observability.
31	///
32	/// This has a hand-written [`Serialize`]/[`Deserialize`] impl rather than a
33	/// derive, so it cannot derive [`specta::Type`] either: nothing here
34	/// introspects its shape for TypeScript. Every field that carries a
35	/// `SystemEvent` is instead given a `#[specta(type = String)]` override at
36	/// the field, matching the plain string it actually serializes as.
37	#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq, Hash)]
38	#[non_exhaustive]
39	pub enum SystemEvent {
40	    /// The Agent Runtime's hosted agent process is up and its ACP channel is
41	    /// wired end-to-end: the Agent Service may now start the ACP
42	    /// `initialize`/`session/new` handshake. Sent at most once per
43	    /// connection, before any ACP traffic.
44	    AcpReady,
45	    /// An application-defined event name with no protocol-level meaning yet.
46	    Unknown(String),
47	}
48	
49	impl SystemEvent {
50	    /// Borrow the wire string for this event name.
51	    #[must_use]
52	    pub fn as_str(&self) -> &str {
53	        match self {
54	            Self::AcpReady => "acp_ready",
55	            Self::Unknown(name) => name,
56	        }
57	    }
58	}
59	
60	impl Serialize for SystemEvent {
61	    fn serialize<S>(&self, serializer: S) -> Result<S::Ok, S::Error>
62	    where
63	        S: Serializer,
64	    {
65	        serializer.serialize_str(self.as_str())
66	    }
67	}
68	
69	impl<'de> Deserialize<'de> for SystemEvent {
70	    fn deserialize<D>(deserializer: D) -> Result<Self, D::Error>
71	    where
72	        D: Deserializer<'de>,
73	    {
74	        Ok(match String::deserialize(deserializer)?.as_str() {
75	            "acp_ready" => Self::AcpReady,
76	            name => Self::Unknown(name.to_owned()),
77	        })
78	    }
79	}
80	
81	/// One complete ACP JSON-RPC message routed between the Agent Service and the
82	/// single agent execution hosted by this connection.
83	///
84	/// Its own JSON-RPC fields are opaque to TypeScript consumers here (typed as
85	/// an arbitrary object of unknown values): they already have a proper ACP SDK
86	/// on the TypeScript side, so this crate only needs to guarantee the message
87	/// round-trips unchanged. This is typed as a map rather than plain `unknown`
88	/// because [`ToRuntimeMessage`]/[`ToServerMessage`] carry it in an internally
89	/// tagged `Acp` variant, which requires its payload provably serialize as an
90	/// object so the `"type"` tag can be merged into it. `#[serde(transparent)]`
91	/// changes nothing about the actual wire format here - a single-field tuple
92	/// struct already serializes transparently by default - but it does tell
93	/// specta's serde-compatibility checker that this newtype is transparent, so
94	/// it looks through to the map type below instead of treating `AcpMessage`
95	/// itself as an opaque, non-mergeable struct.
96	#[derive(Debug, Clone, Serialize, Deserialize, Type)]
97	#[serde(transparent)]
98	pub struct AcpMessage(
99	    #[specta(type = std::collections::HashMap<String, Unknown>)] pub RawJsonRpcMessage,
100	);
101	
102	/// Agent Service to Agent Runtime traffic on the logical protocol stream.
103	#[derive(Debug, Clone, Serialize, Deserialize, Type)]
104	#[serde(tag = "type", rename_all = "camelCase")]
105	#[non_exhaustive]
106	pub enum ToRuntimeMessage {
107	    /// An ACP message routed to the hosted agent.
108	    Acp(AcpMessage),
109	}
110	
111	/// Agent Runtime to Agent Service traffic on the logical protocol stream.
112	#[derive(Debug, Clone, Serialize, Deserialize, Type)]
113	#[serde(tag = "type", rename_all = "camelCase")]
114	#[non_exhaustive]
115	pub enum ToServerMessage {
116	    /// An ACP message routed from the hosted agent.
117	    Acp(AcpMessage),
118	    /// A runtime or agent lifecycle event.
119	    Event {
120	        /// The event name.
121	        #[specta(type = String)]
122	        event: SystemEvent,
123	    },
124	}

22	/// The kind of runtime or agent state transition reported to the Agent Service.
23	///
24	/// The protocol does not define a full event-name catalog yet, so this enum
25	/// is non-exhaustive: unrecognized wire strings still round-trip losslessly
26	/// through [`SystemEvent::Unknown`]. [`SystemEvent::AcpReady`] is the one
27	/// name the Agent Service actually acts on (see
28	/// `agent_proxy::inbound::runtime::RuntimeConnectionDriver`, which waits for
29	/// it before starting the ACP `initialize`/`session/new` handshake) rather
30	/// than merely forwarding it for observability.
31	///
32	/// This has a hand-written [`Serialize`]/[`Deserialize`] impl rather than a
33	/// derive, so it cannot derive [`specta::Type`] either: nothing here
34	/// introspects its shape for TypeScript. Every field that carries a
35	/// `SystemEvent` is instead given a `#[specta(type = String)]` override at
36	/// the field, matching the plain string it actually serializes as.
37	#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq, Hash)]
38	#[non_exhaustive]
39	pub enum SystemEvent {
40	    /// The Agent Runtime's hosted agent process is up and its ACP channel is
41	    /// wired end-to-end: the Agent Service may now start the ACP
42	    /// `initialize`/`session/new` handshake. Sent at most once per
43	    /// connection, before any ACP traffic.
44	    AcpReady,
45	    /// An application-defined event name with no protocol-level meaning yet.
46	    Unknown(String),
47	}
48	
49	impl SystemEvent {
50	    /// Borrow the wire string for this event name.
51	    #[must_use]
52	    pub fn as_str(&self) -> &str {
53	        match self {
54	            Self::AcpReady => "acp_ready",
55	            Self::Unknown(name) => name,
56	        }
57	    }
58	}
59	
60	impl Serialize for SystemEvent {
61	    fn serialize<S>(&self, serializer: S) -> Result<S::Ok, S::Error>
62	    where
63	        S: Serializer,
64	    {
65	        serializer.serialize_str(self.as_str())
66	    }
67	}
68	
69	impl<'de> Deserialize<'de> for SystemEvent {
70	    fn deserialize<D>(deserializer: D) -> Result<Self, D::Error>
71	    where
72	        D: Deserializer<'de>,
73	    {
74	        Ok(match String::deserialize(deserializer)?.as_str() {
75	            "acp_ready" => Self::AcpReady,
76	            name => Self::Unknown(name.to_owned()),
77	        })
78	    }
79	}
80	
81	/// One complete ACP JSON-RPC message routed between the Agent Service and the
82	/// single agent execution hosted by this connection.
83	///
84	/// Its own JSON-RPC fields are opaque to TypeScript consumers here (typed as
85	/// an arbitrary object of unknown values): they already have a proper ACP SDK
86	/// on the TypeScript side, so this crate only needs to guarantee the message
87	/// round-trips unchanged. This is typed as a map rather than plain `unknown`
88	/// because [`ToRuntimeMessage`]/[`ToServerMessage`] carry it in an internally
89	/// tagged `Acp` variant, which requires its payload provably serialize as an
90	/// object so the `"type"` tag can be merged into it. `#[serde(transparent)]`
91	/// changes nothing about the actual wire format here - a single-field tuple
92	/// struct already serializes transparently by default - but it does tell
93	/// specta's serde-compatibility checker that this newtype is transparent, so
94	/// it looks through to the map type below instead of treating `AcpMessage`
95	/// itself as an opaque, non-mergeable struct.
96	#[derive(Debug, Clone, Serialize, Deserialize, Type)]
97	#[serde(transparent)]
98	pub struct AcpMessage(
99	    #[specta(type = std::collections::HashMap<String, Unknown>)] pub RawJsonRpcMessage,
100	);

102	/// Agent Service to Agent Runtime traffic on the logical protocol stream.
103	#[derive(Debug, Clone, Serialize, Deserialize, Type)]
104	#[serde(tag = "type", rename_all = "camelCase")]
105	#[non_exhaustive]
106	pub enum ToRuntimeMessage {
107	    /// An ACP message routed to the hosted agent.
108	    Acp(AcpMessage),
109	}
110	
111	/// Agent Runtime to Agent Service traffic on the logical protocol stream.
112	#[derive(Debug, Clone, Serialize, Deserialize, Type)]
113	#[serde(tag = "type", rename_all = "camelCase")]
114	#[non_exhaustive]
115	pub enum ToServerMessage {
116	    /// An ACP message routed from the hosted agent.
117	    Acp(AcpMessage),
118	    /// A runtime or agent lifecycle event.
119	    Event {
120	        /// The event name.
121	        #[specta(type = String)]

Read the relevant code. Short answer: **the gating logic is easy (~10 lines); the cost is structural plumbing in `agent_harness`, roughly a half-day.**

## What already exists

`agent_proxy` does exactly this today — `crates/agent_proxy/src/inbound/runtime.rs:123-147` waits for `SystemEvent::AcpReady` on the event channel and only then spawns `handle_agent_connected` (which runs `initialize`/`session/new`). The comment there is even the rationale you just described. So there's a proven pattern to copy.

## What's missing in `agent_harness`

Three things block a direct copy:

1. **No initialize at all.** `AgentSessionImpl` (`domain/agent_sessions/session.rs:34-40`) is a pass-through `send`/`receive` over the transport. Nothing in the harness sends an ACP handshake yet, so "wait, then initialize" means writing the initialize half too.

2. **`create_session` is sync.** `AgentSessionManager::create_session(&mut self, &AgentSessionId) -> &T` (`manager.rs:11`) can't await. Any waiting version either makes it `async` or moves the wait behind the session.

3. **Receive is pull-based and single-consumer.** `session.receive()` reads the raw transport directly. If creation loops on `recv()` waiting for the `Event`, it swallows any `Acp` frames that arrive first, and nobody else can read concurrently. You need a demux — one loop draining the transport, routing `Event{..}` → readiness signal, `Acp(..)` → the ACP side.

## Cheapest path

Don't hand-roll the demux — `agent_runtime_protocol::domain::connection::ServerConnection::connect` (`connection/mod.rs:59`) already does it: give it the channel and a `SystemEventHandler`, get back a real `agent_client_protocol::Channel`. Your handler flips a `tokio::sync::watch<bool>` on `AcpReady`.

Then pick where the wait lives:

- **Gate inside the session** (recommended): `create_session` stays sync and returns immediately; `send()` awaits the ready watch before writing, and the pump fires initialize once on the ready edge. Callers never see the gate, tests stay synchronous-ish. ~60–80 lines.
- **Async `create_session`**: smaller diff (~30 lines) but the manager blocks on a container that may never boot, and you need a timeout + a story for a container that dies pre-ready.

One open question that decides the shape: should `send()` on a not-yet-ready session **await**, **queue** (agent_proxy durably queues, per `service.rs:138-142`), or **error**? Which do you want?

content.text:
Scoped it. `agent_proxy` isn't just a crate — it's a deployed vertical slice. Here's the full surface:

## What "delete agent_proxy" actually touches

**Rust (safe, reversible via git)**
- `crates/agent_proxy` — 19 files, 3,790 lines (929-line domain service + 1,073-line test file)
- `services/agent_proxy_service` — 168 lines, the only reverse-dep of the lib
- 2 entries in root `Cargo.toml`, plus `Cargo.lock`
- `crates/macro_service_urls/src/lib.rs:540-544` — the `wss://agent-proxy{-dev}.macro.com` runtime URL
- 3 `.sqlx/query-*.json` cache entries

**Generated / cross-language**
- `packages/sdk`: `'agent-proxy'` in the service union (`config.ts:18`), 3 base URLs, `services.ts`, `specs/agent-proxy.json` — **this is a breaking change for SDK consumers**
- `apps/web/src/lib/service-clients/service-agent-proxy/` — 39 generated files + an `orval.config.ts` entry. Good news: **zero hand-written web code imports it**, so it's a pure generated-artifact delete.
- `.github/workspace-dep-closures.json`, `docker/docker-compose.yml`, `docker/Dockerfile.dev`, `infra/local/generated/acp/*`

**Deployed state — I won't touch this without an explicit go**
- `infra/stacks/agent-proxy-service/` has `Pulumi.dev.yaml` **and `Pulumi.prod.yaml`** — there's a live prod service. Deleting the stack source orphans real cloud resources; they need `pulumi destroy` first, by you.
- `infra/stacks/doppler-projects/index.ts` has an agent-proxy project.
- `crates/macro_db_client/migrations/20260729215917_agent_proxy_pending_messages.sql` — **already applied**. Deleting an applied migration breaks every environment's migration ledger. The right move is a new `DROP TABLE` migration, not a file delete.

## Two things worth deciding before I start

1. **`agent_harness` is not close to parity.** Its whole domain is ~200 lines of session/container scaffolding. `agent_proxy` carries the ACP handshake, the `AcpReady` gate you just asked about, the pending-message queue, turn accumulation, chat persistence, and 5 HTTP routes (`/agents`, `/sessions/{id}/acp`, `/runtime` WS upgrade). Deleting it now also deletes the reference implementation for the feature in your previous message. Only doc comments in `agent_harness` reference it — no code coupling — so it can stay around harmlessly while you port.

2. **Scope.** Which do you want?
   - **(a) Full teardown now** — everything above except infra-destroy and the migration, which I'd stage as a drop-migration and a written handoff for you to run.
   - **(b) Code-only** — delete the crate + service + Cargo/SDK/web wiring, leave `infra/` and the migration entirely alone for a later pass.
   - **(c) Port first** — I lift the `AcpReady` gate and handshake into `agent_harness`, get it working, *then* we delete.

My read is **(c) then (a)** — but if `agent_harness_service` is already the intended replacement and you just want the dead weight gone, (b) is a clean single commit. Which way?
we're going ot be totally reshaping how the system works. we will NO LONGER proxy to chat. we're going to use the new
[@/home/wolf/Macro/repos/wolf-2/crates/agent_session/](file:///home/wolf/Macro/repos/wolf-2/crates/agent_session/)
instead. and we're going to hvae it so that agent session persists all the ACP. i want to chat about this
Let me read `agent_session` so I'm grounded before we talk.

Read it all. Good news first: **`agent_session` is already shaped for this.** `AgentSessionLog { agent_session_id, user_id, content: Message }` with `Message::ToServer | ToRuntime` persisted as `direction` + `content` JSONB round-trips whole protocol envelopes losslessly. You're not designing the persistence model — it exists. What you're deciding is what it *means*.

Here's what I think the real questions are.

## 1. Is the log the source of truth, or an audit trail?

This is the fork everything else hangs off.

`agent_proxy` had `translate.rs` + `TurnAccumulator` because ACP arrives as a stream of deltas and chat needs coherent messages. If you delete the proxy, that fold has to live *somewhere* — you've moved it, not removed it. Three places it can go:

- **Client-side fold.** Log is truth, UI replays raw ACP. Cleanest server, but ACP semantics leak into the frontend and every client reimplements the fold.
- **Derived projection.** Log is truth, a projector writes a read model. Most work, best reads, and replayable when the fold logic changes.
- **In-memory fold + snapshot.** Log is the write-ahead record, live state is memory, periodic snapshot. Fast, but a restart mid-turn has to replay.

Which one do you have in mind? I'd guess you're leaning at the first, and it's defensible for a coding agent where the "chat" is really a transcript.

## 2. Volume — this is the one that'll bite

ACP `session/update` notifications stream at roughly token granularity. One `INSERT` per envelope means **thousands of rows per turn**, each with a JSONB payload, on the hot path of a live stream. `AgentSessionLogRepo::create` is one-row-at-a-time with no batching.

Do you want *literally* all ACP, or all ACP *except* streaming deltas? "Persist every request/response and every terminal notification, drop the intermediate text chunks" gets you 95% of the replay value at 1% of the rows. If you do want the deltas, this needs batched or async-buffered writes before it goes near production.

## 3. Ordering is currently broken for this use case

`agent_session_log` orders by `(created_at, id)` — and `id` is a random UUID. Two rows written in the same microsecond tie-break **randomly**, which for a token stream means scrambled output. You need a monotonic `BIGSERIAL seq` (or per-session counter) as the real order key. Small migration, but it's load-bearing the moment the log becomes the transcript.

## 4. What still reaches the channel thread?

`AgentSession` keeps `created_from_thread_id` *and* its own `thread_id`. So a comms thread still exists — meaning "no longer proxy to chat" presumably means *no chat-message proxy crate*, not *no thread output*. Someone still has to post something human-readable into that thread when the agent replies. Is that a thin projector off the log, or does the agent explicitly emit "post this to the thread" actions?

## 5. Does the log make sessions resumable?

If a container dies mid-session, can you spawn a new one and replay the log into it to reconstitute state? If **yes**, the log must be complete and exact, and that kills the filtering idea in #2. If **no** — it's a transcript, resume is the harness's problem via `acp_session_id` — you have much more freedom. This one constrains #2, so it's worth answering first.

---

My instinct: **log everything except streaming text deltas, add a `seq` column, fold client-side, treat resume as out of scope for v1.** But #5 is the question that decides it — where's your head at on resumability?

That settles it — server-side fold, log as truth, and the session auto-persists. That's a coherent design and it's the one I'd pick. Three things get sharper as a consequence.

## The black box has one hole: `user_id` attribution

`AgentSessionLog.user_id` is `Some` only when the ACP originated from a user. If persistence is a side effect of `LiveAgentSession::send`, then `send()` has to know *who* — and today it takes only a message.

So the black box can't be fully blind. Either:

```rust
async fn send(&self, from: Option<MacroUserIdStr<'static>>, message: ToRuntimeMessage) -> ...
```

or two doors — `send(msg)` for harness-originated traffic, `send_from_user(user, msg)` for user-originated. I lean at the second: the call sites genuinely are two different things (a user prompt vs. the harness's own `initialize`), and the type makes you say which. `receive()` is always `user_id: None`, so it stays clean either way.

## `create` flexibility — what I think you actually need

Four pressures on that trait, in the order they'll hurt:

```rust

    /// session_id + id are implied by the owner, not passed in
    fn append(&self, entry: NewLogEntry) -> impl Future<Output = Result<LogSeq>> + Send;

    fn append_many(&self, entries: Vec<NewLogEntry>) -> impl Future<Output = Result<LogSeq>> + Send;

    fn list_by_session(
        &self,
        agent_session_id: AgentSessionId,
        after: Option<LogSeq>,
        limit: u32,
    ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Vec<AgentSessionLog>>> + Send;
}
```

- **`NewLogEntry` instead of `AgentSessionLog`** — a session that owns its repo already knows its own id; making it restate it invites mismatch. Same reasoning as `NewAgentSession` vs `AgentSession`, which you already applied one layer up.
- **Returns `LogSeq`** — you need a monotonic cursor, and append is the natural place to mint it.
- **`append_many`** — one INSERT per token-delta on the live path won't hold up. Even if v1 doesn't batch, having the door means adding buffering later isn't a trait change.
- **Cursor on `list_by_session`** — unbounded `Vec` is fine for the mock and fatal for the fold endpoint on a long session. This is also what lets the fold be incremental instead of re-reading from zero.

And the ordering point from before is now load-bearing rather than theoretical: `ORDER BY created_at, id` with a random UUID tiebreak will scramble same-microsecond writes. `LogSeq` as `BIGSERIAL` solves the cursor and the ordering in one migration.

## The manager signature has to change more than you might expect

Two independent forces:

**Postgres makes it async and fallible.** `create_session(&mut self, id: &AgentSessionId) -> &T` → probably `create_session(&self, new: NewAgentSession) -> Result<Arc<T>>`, taking `NewAgentSession` because `AgentSessionRepo::create` mints the id and thread rather than accepting them.

**`&mut self -> &T` won't survive concurrency.** Your own note on `AgentSessionRepo` says callers drive sessions from spawned tasks. A returned `&T` borrows the manager for the reference's whole life, so no second task can touch it. That wants `&self` + interior mutability, handing out `Arc<T>`.

Worth being explicit about the split: **postgres owns session identity and the log; memory owns the live transport.** A live container connection can't be persisted, so the manager is a postgres-backed registry *plus* an in-memory map of currently-attached connections. Restart = rows survive, connections don't. That's also where your `AcpReady` gate from earlier lands naturally — the row exists immediately, the connection becomes usable later.

## On the fold

Keep it a pure function — `fold(&[AgentSessionLog]) -> MessageChain`, no I/O, no repo. Then it's trivially testable against fixtures, you can iterate the fold logic without touching storage, and re-folding after a logic change is just a re-read. Doesn't need to exist now; just don't let it grow tendrils into the repo when it does.

Good — that constraint actually decides the architecture, and it points somewhere specific.

## The testability idea, taken seriously

If tests drive everything manually, the honest move is a **sans-io core**: the state machine is a plain synchronous struct that takes events and returns actions. No async, no transport, no mocks.

```rust
enum Action {
    Send(ToRuntimeMessage),
    Log(NewLogEntry),
    SetAcpSessionId(AcpId),
}

impl SessionCore {
    fn on_inbound(&mut self, msg: ToServerMessage) -> Vec<Action>;
    fn on_send(&mut self, from: Option<UserId>, msg: ToRuntimeMessage) -> Vec<Action>;
}
```

Then a test is just:

```rust
let mut core = SessionCore::booting();
assert!(core.on_send(user, prompt).is_empty());          // buffered
let actions = core.on_inbound(acp_ready());              // -> [Send(initialize)]
let actions = core.on_inbound(initialize_response());    // -> [Send(session/new)]
let actions = core.on_inbound(session_new_response());   // -> [SetAcpSessionId, Send(prompt)]
```

The reason this matters more than "don't spawn the pump": `begin_handshake` as I sketched it does real ACP round-trips inline. Even without a pump, a test would need a fake ACP client to get past `AcpReady`. Sans-io deletes that problem — the handshake responses are just more `on_inbound` calls. The cost is that request-id correlation becomes explicit state instead of hiding inside `.await`, but that complexity is real either way; this just makes it visible.

The async pump then becomes ~15 lines that execute `Action`s, and it's the only part that isn't unit-testable.

**`ContainerManager::resume`** in `containers.rs:10` now has a job. `ChannelEvent` means the row exists but the container probably doesn't — sandboxes get stopped or archived. So `ChannelEvent` is: look up session → no live container → resume or re-spawn → wire → `send_message` (buffers) → wait for ready → handshake → flush. Same tail as `NewSession`, different head. That's a nice property: one boot path, two entry points.

**But it forks the handshake.** `AgentSession.acp_session_id: Option<String>` exists exactly for this, and now I see why:

- `NewSession` → `acp_session_id` is `None` → `initialize` then **`session/new`**
- `ChannelEvent` resume → `acp_session_id` is `Some` → `initialize` then **`session/load`**

So `Handshaking` branches on the stored id. Worth building that in from the start rather than retrofitting — it's one match arm now and a surgery later. Does the container actually preserve enough state for `session/load` to work after a sandbox restart, or does resume in practice mean "new ACP session, replay context from the log"? That changes which one we call.

**One gap left.** `NewSession` carries three thread ids and no `message_id`. But the message that triggered it was posted *before* the session existed, so it can't arrive as a `ChannelEvent` either. So on `NewSession` we must go read the thread ourselves to build the first prompt — meaning a "read thread contents" outbound port, and `sub_thread_id`/`top_level_thread_id` are what we read. //! Bridge a sidecar WebSocket to typed ACP frames.
//!
//! Shared by both providers: Daytona dials the sidecar through a preview URL
//! and Namespace through an ingress, but past the dial the protocol is
//! identical, so the pump is written once here.
//!
//! ## One message, one frame
//!
//! There is no buffering, splitting, or partial-line handling, because the
//! sidecar does not stream bytes. `container/sidecar` reads the agent's stdout
//! with `BufReader::lines()` and sends each complete line as one WebSocket
//! text message; WebSocket is message-oriented and tungstenite reassembles
//! fragmented frames before yielding a `Message`. So every message that
//! arrives is exactly one JSON value.
//!
//! The same holds outbound, with one wrinkle worth not re-learning: the
//! sidecar appends the newline to the agent's stdin itself, so frames are sent
//! *without* a trailing newline. Adding one here puts a blank line into the
//! agent's stdin after every frame.
//!
//! If the sidecar ever becomes a genuine byte pipe, this is where the framing
//! would come back - and at that point `tokio_util::codec` over
//! `ws_stream_tungstenite` is a better answer than a hand-rolled buffer.

use agent_client_protocol::RawJsonRpcMessage;
use agent_runtime_protocol::domain::channel::Channel;
use futures::{SinkExt, StreamExt};
use tokio::io::{AsyncRead, AsyncWrite};
use tokio_tungstenite::WebSocketStream;
use tokio_tungstenite::tungstenite::Message;

use crate::domain::ports::AcpFrames;

/// Wire a connected sidecar socket to a channel of typed ACP frames.
///
/// Returns the caller's end; the pump runs on its own task until either side
/// closes.
pub fn spawn<Socket>(socket: WebSocketStream<Socket>) -> AcpFrames
where
    Socket: AsyncRead + AsyncWrite + Unpin + Send + 'static,
{
    let (ours, theirs) = Channel::duplex();
    tokio::spawn(pump(socket, theirs));
    ours
}

/// Relay frames until either side closes.
async fn pump<Socket>(
    socket: WebSocketStream<Socket>,
    side: Channel<RawJsonRpcMessage, RawJsonRpcMessage>,
) where
    Socket: AsyncRead + AsyncWrite + Unpin + Send + 'static,
{
    let (mut socket_tx, mut socket_rx) = socket.split();
    let Channel { tx, mut rx } = side;

    loop {
        tokio::select! {
            outbound = rx.recv() => {
                let Some(frame) = outbound else { break };
                // A frame we just built failing to serialize is not worth
                // tearing the session down over.
                let Ok(json) = serde_json::to_string(&frame) else {
                    tracing::error!("could not serialize an outgoing acp frame");
                    continue;
                };
                if socket_tx.send(Message::Text(json.into())).await.is_err() {
                    break;
                }
            }
            inbound = socket_rx.next() => {
                let json = match inbound {
                    Some(Ok(Message::Text(text))) => text.to_string(),
                    Some(Ok(Message::Binary(data))) => match String::from_utf8(data.to_vec()) {
                        Ok(text) => text,
                        Err(error) => {
                            tracing::error!(?error, "agent sent a non-utf8 acp frame");
                            continue;
                        }
                    },
                    // Not part of the protocol.
                    Some(Ok(Message::Ping(_) | Message::Pong(_) | Message::Frame(_))) => continue,
                    Some(Ok(Message::Close(_)) | Err(_)) | None => break,
                };

                match serde_json::from_str::<RawJsonRpcMessage>(&json) {
                    Ok(frame) => {
                        if tx.send(frame).is_err() {
                            break;
                        }
                    }
                    // One unparseable frame is not fatal: the agent keeps
                    // talking, and dropping the session would lose the rest.
                    Err(error) => {
                        tracing::error!(?error, %json, "agent sent an unparseable acp frame");
                    }
                }
            }
        }
    }
    tracing::debug!("sidecar pump finished");
}

issue using Honeycomb. Examples:

<commentary>

run queries, use BubbleUp, trace analysis, and report findings.
</commentary>
</example>

<example>
Context: User sees errors in production after a deployment
user: "We deployed v2.5 and errors spiked. Investigate what went wrong in Honeycomb."
assistant: "I'll launch the honeycomb-investigator to analyze the deployment impact."
<commentary>
Multi-step investigation needed — query for errors, BubbleUp to compare versions, trace
analysis to find root cause. Agent orchestrates the full workflow.
</commentary>
</example>

<example>
Context: SLO budget is burning fast
user: "Our checkout SLO is burning budget fast. Can you figure out what's going on?"

options.name: honeycomb:instrumentation-advisor
options.description:
Use this agent when the user wants to improve their application's observability by analyzing
their codebase against what Honeycomb actually receives. This agent autonomously scans code,
queries Honeycomb for existing coverage, and produces a prioritized gap analysis with
ready-to-apply code. Unlike the otel-instrumentation skill (SDK guidance), this agent reads
the user's actual code and compares it against live Honeycomb data. Examples:

<example>
Context: User wants to know what they should instrument next
user: "What's missing from our instrumentation? We have basic tracing but I feel like we're not getting enough detail."
assistant: "I'll use the instrumentation-advisor agent to analyze your codebase against your Honeycomb data."
<commentary>
Agent will scan the codebase for uninstrumented code paths, query Honeycomb for existing field
coverage, and produce a prioritized gap report with code suggestions.
</commentary>
</example>

<example>
Context: User wants to add observability to a specific service
user: "Can you instrument our checkout service? It's in Go and we have basic OTel but no custom spans."
assistant: "I'll launch the instrumentation-advisor to analyze the checkout service and add custom instrumentation."
<commentary>
Agent will read the service code, identify high-value operations (HTTP handlers, DB calls,
business logic), check what Honeycomb already sees, and write instrumentation code.
</commentary>
</example>

<example>
Context: User is debugging and notices gaps in their traces
user: "Our traces are missing context — I can't tell which user or tenant is affected. Can you fix that?"
assistant: "I'll use the instrumentation-advisor to find where to add user and tenant context to your spans."
<commentary>
Attribute enrichment task. Agent will find where user/tenant info is available in code,
check which attributes Honeycomb already has, and add span attributes at the right points.
</commentary>
</example>

content.text: Good call — four things in there, and one of them reverses a decision I'

d leaned on.

## Lift wholesale

**`AcpSessionId`** (`models.rs`) is our `AcpId`
, already finished: `new(impl Into<String>)`, `as_str()`, `into_string()`, `Display`, serde, and a doc comment explaining why it must

never be interchangeable with the session id. Ours is `pub struct AcpId(String);` and nothing else. Straight lift.

**`translate.rs`
+ its 125-line test** is the fold you described — `translate_session_update`, `content_block_text`, and `TurnAccumulator` which merges consecutive text
/thinking chunks into one coherent part. That's the "FOLD the log into a nice message chain" endpoint, already written and

tested. It's currently only in git history; worth rescuing before it's forgotten.

**Confirmed import path:** `agent_client
_protocol::schema::v1::{ContentBlock, SessionUpdate, ToolCall, ToolCallStatus, ToolCallUpdate}`. So typed-

all-the-way-down is real, and `translate.rs` is the working example of it.

## The one that changes a decision

The `

agent_proxy_pending_message` migration comment states the semantics outright:

> rows survive restarts and reconnects so a prompt

posted before the runtime exists is never lost

So the old system deliberately made the pre-ready buffer **durable**. My
sketch has it in memory with log-at-flush — which silently loses a user's prompt if the process dies while the

container boots. That's a regression from what you already built.

Since the log is now source of truth, the f
ix doesn't need a second table: **log at enqueue, and the log becomes the buffer.** On restart, replay the log,

find prompts with no corresponding response, re-send. No `pending_message` table at all.

Cost: the log records
intent rather than pure wire traffic, so `transcript()` in the integration test gains a `to_runtime(SessionP
rompt)` entry *before* `acp_ready` instead of after the handshake. That flips the assertion I show
ed you. It's the more correct behaviour though — and it means the durable-

buffer property comes free from a table we're already writing.

## Proposed first step
Smaller than the mocks, and it unblocks everything else: **lift `AcpSessionId` into `domain/acp_id.rs
`**. The state machine's `Live { acp_session_id }` and `SetAcpSessionId` both need a us

able type, and right now there isn't one.

Alongside it, rescue `translate.rs` + `
translate/test.rs` into the crate unregistered, so the fold work later doesn't start from

scratch — same treatment as `daytona.rs`.

Then mocks, then types

+ failing test, then the state machine.

content.text: Green

, formatted, no new lints. Here's what the helpers look like:

```
cr

ates/agent_harness/src/testing/
  mod.rs                 pub mod helpers;
  helpers/
    mod.rs
    agent.rs             FakeAgent

— raw ACP only
    container.rs         ContainerMock  — envelope boundary, awaits properly
    log.rs

LogRepoMock    — AgentSessionLogRepo in memory
    transcript.rs        Direction / AcpMethod / FrameKind / T

ranscriptEntry
```

**`FakeAgent`** — the agent process. Knows nothing of the `agent-runtime.v0` env
elope; reads and writes complete JSON-RPC values, exactly like the real sidecar's st

dout.

```rust
agent.sends_reply(id, result);        agent.received

_frames()  -> Vec<RawJsonRpcMessage>
agent.sends_error(id, acp_error);     agent.received_k

inds()   -> Vec<FrameKind>
agent.sends_notification(m, params);  agent.received_methods() -> Vec<AcpMethod>
```
**`ContainerMock`** — owns a `FakeAgent` and is the envelope boundary: wraps agent frames as `
ToServerMessage::Acp`, originates `Event` itself. `sends_ready()` / `sends_event

(..)` / `disconnects()` / `sent()`.

Backed by two mpsc channels behind one `select!`, so **`recv()` genuin
ely awaits**. The old version returned `Ok(None)` on an empty queue, which `Transport`
defines as "counterpart closed" — a forgotten enqueue now hangs (pointing at the missing call) inst

ead of silently looking like a dead container. Only `disconnects()` ends the stream.

**Typed transcript, no arrows.** `received_methods()`
returns `Vec<AcpMethod>`, so assertions are `[AcpMethod::Initialize, AcpMethod::SessionNew]` — a renamed method is a compile error.

`log.transcript()` gives `Vec<TranscriptEntry>` carrying `Direction` + `FrameKind`.

Both `

ContainerMock` and `LogRepoMock` are `Clone` with shared interiors, so a test keeps its handle after moving them into a session.

Two things I h

it worth knowing:

- **`RequestId` lives at `agent_client_protocol::schema::v1::RequestId`**, not the cr
ate root. Also confirmed the workspace is on `agent-client-protocol` **1.2.0** / schema **1

.4.0** — I'd been reading 1.3.0/1.5.0 docs earlier, so ignore anything I said sourced from those.
- **
`ToServerMessage`/`ToRuntimeMessage` are `#[non_exhaustive]`**, so downstream matches need wildcards. `TranscriptE
ntry::of` panics with the offending value on an unhandled variant — a new protocol variant should force a helper update rather than silently

projecting wrong.

I updated `managed_session_speaks_to_its_container` for the new API and it still passes —

that's the proof this step works, since nothing here is `todo!()`.

Next step as disc
ussed: `AcpId` lifted from `AcpSessionId`, `SessionState`, the `AgentSessionImpl::new` signature, and
the integration test — compiling and failing honestly. Want me to go?

were right — that was hand-rolled duplication of something the library owns. Fixed:

```rust
if
l_jsonrpc_request_enum!` (`schema/enum_impls.rs:13`), e.g. `N
ewSessionRequest => "session/new"`, and `JsonRpcMessage::matches_method` reads them. Test still passes, no new l
ints — the 3 remaining are your pre-existing unused re-exports and the `from_id` na

ming.

## Why I stopped at the projection rather than parsing into `

ClientRequest`

I looked at going all the way — `FrameKind`

holding actual `ClientRequest` / `AgentNotification` values. Two things make that a bigger change than it looks:

**Dire
ction determines which enum to parse into.** There are two request enums with overlapping roles: `ClientRequ
est` (`initialize`, `session/new`, `session/prompt` — what the harness sends) and `AgentRequest` (`fs/read_
text_file`, `session/request_permission`, `terminal/create` — what the agent sends *back* to us). Same wire shape, different me
aning by role. So `FrameKind::of(frame)` can't type a frame without also being told the direction — which is in

herent to ACP, not an artifact of my design.

**Responses can't be parsed standalone.** `Response<Result, Error>` is `#[
serde(untagged)]`, and `AgentResponse` is keyed by *method* (`impl_jsonrpc_response_enum!`, `:
32`). So typing a response requires correlating its id back to the originating request's method. The transcript de

liberately keeps `Response { id }` payload-free, which sidesteps that entirely.

**And it
would make assertions worse.** Holding full payloads means constructing a whole `InitializeRequest` in the test to compare against
. `AcpMethod` is lossy on purpose so `[AcpMethod::Initialize, AcpMethod::SessionNew

]` stays readable.

Where full typing *does* belong is the state machine: when we build `
initialize`/`session/new`/`session/load` we should construct real `ClientRequest` values and ser
ialize them, and parse the replies as `AgentResponse` — the library's `parse_message` hand

les both. That's the next step, and there the payloads matter.

That direction-pl
us-correlation constraint is also a hint about the state machine itself: it has
to track which id it sent which method with, or it can't type
the response it gets back. Which is the request-id counter we already
said it needs.

content.text: Hon
est answer: we don't need it, and it only exists because I invented `
AcpMethod` first and then needed a way to populate it. That's backwards — the library already has the enums

.

`from_wire` exists purely so `received_methods()` and `transcript()` could return something
comparable for assertions. It's a projection I introduced, and it duplicates `impl_jsonrp

c_request_enum!`.

## The better way

`JsonRpcMessage::parse_message(method, params)` parses a raw frame straight into the library's own enum
. And the mock already knows the direction — `FakeAgent` only ever receives client→agent traffic — so it can pick the right en

ading as a sequence:

```rust
assert!(matches!(
    agent.received_requests().as_slice(),
    [
        ClientRequest::InitializeRequest(_),
, no strings, and a renamed variant is a compile error rather than a silent mismatch. `AcpMethod` and `from_wire` both get

deleted.

## The one place it doesn't fully collapse

Three library enums, not one

, and they're split by role and by kind:

| | harness → agent | agent → harness |
|---|---|---|
| requests |

`ClientRequest` | `AgentRequest` |
| notifications | `ClientNotification` | `AgentNotification` |
| responses | `ClientResponse` | `AgentResponse`

|

For `FakeAgent` that's fine — it's always the agent side,

so `received_requests()` is unambiguous.

For `transcript()` it
's messier, because one `Vec` mixes all of it. And responses are
the genuinely awkward case: `Response<Result, Error>` is `#[serde(untagged)]` and `AgentRes
ponse` is keyed by method, so a response can't be typed without correlating its id back to the request that caused it — which

the log helper doesn't track.

So the transcript is either:

```rust
pub enum TranscriptEntry {
    Event(SystemEvent),
    To

Agent(ClientRequest),
    FromAgent(AgentNotification),
    FromAgentRequest(AgentRequest),
    /// Responses carry no method of their own.
    Response(

RequestId),
}
```

…which is honest but has that one lossy variant, or the
log helper starts tracking outstanding request ids so it can name responses too — real

correlation logic inside a test helper, which I'd rather not have.

My
call: **delete `AcpMethod`/`from_wire`, go typed via `parse_message`
, and accept `Response(RequestId)` as lossy.** The state machine's own corre
lation is what we actually want to test, so a helper that independ

ently reimplements it would be testing itself.

Want me to make that change now? And do
you care about naming responses in the transcript, or is id-only fine there?

the variant name — rather than a field. Payloads are the ACP crate's own enums, parsed via `JsonRpcM
essage::parse_message`, so the library owns every method string. One generic does all

otification>` — no `Direction` plumbing needed, because the agent side only ever sees client-to-agent traffic

content.text: Not
a bad idea at all — it's a clear improvement, and the type system pushed it further than I expected.

```rust
pub fn sends_reply<R>(&self, id: RequestId, response: R)
where
    R: JsonRpcResponse + serde::Serial

ize,

pub fn sends_notification<N>(&self, notification: N)
where
    N: JsonRpcNotification + serde::Serialize,
```

Call sites become:

otification::new(..));
```

Verified compiling and passing with a real `NewSessionResponse`.

**Three things that made this

work out better than a plain typed param:**

`JsonRpcResponse` is the right bound because **`serde_json::
Value` implements it** (`jsonrpc.rs:2952`). So one method covers both the typed happy path and the de
liberately-malformed case — no separate `sends_raw_reply`. The bound constrains you to ACP response types while

leaving `json!(..)` available on purpose.

**`sends_notification` no longer takes a method name at all.** `JsonR
pcNotification: JsonRpcMessage` gives `.method()`, so the name comes off the value's own type. That

was the last method string at a call site.

**The response payloads are
`#[non_exhaustive]`** (e.g. `NewSessionResponse`, `agent.rs:1085`), so a struct literal is
n't even legal from our crate — you *must* go through `NewSessionResponse::new(session_id)
` plus its builder methods (`.modes(..)`, `.config_options(..)`). Which means typ
ed construction isn't just nicer here, it's the only path the library all

ows.

I did keep `sends_raw(RawJsonRpcMessage)` for the case neither bound covers — an
agent emitting something that isn't a well-formed response or notification at all. `sidecar_pump.
rs` explicitly tolerates unparseable frames, so that behaviour deserves a test e

ventually.

`sends_error` stays as-is, taking an `AcpError` — errors aren't method

-keyed, so there's nothing to type against.

Test passes, formatted, no new lints.
Next up is the `AcpId` lift + `SessionState` + the failing integration test, unless you want to keep pol
ishing the helpers.

prompt.text: is the agent designed in a way where we can use it to test the sidecar?

content.text: Not as it stands, and the coupling is specific:
**`FakeAgent` doesn't own its own pipe.** `ContainerMock::new` creates the channel and keeps the receiving end

:

```rust
let (frame_tx, frame_rx) = unbounded_channel();
FakeAgent::new(frame_tx),                    // ag

ent gets only the sender
inbound: ... Inbound { frames: frame_rx },   // container

keeps the receiver
```

So the agent can *emit* but nothing can read from it
except the container it was born into. And `deliver()` is `pub(crate)`, called by `ContainerMock::

send`. To drive a sidecar you'd need both halves as a public seam.

What *is*
reusable is the valuable part — typed construction via `sends_reply`/`sends_notification`, the rec

ording, and the `received_requests()` assertions. None of that is mpsc-specific. Only the plumbing is.

## The ref

actor that would open it up

Give `FakeAgent` both ends of its own channel and expose the seam:

```rust
` awaits `next_outbound()` and wraps as `ToServerMess
age::Acp`; its `send()` calls `deliver()`. A sidecar test would be a second, ~20-
line driver: read WS text → `deliver(parse(text))`, and `next_outbound()`

→ WS text.

That's a genuinely nice payoff, because the properties `

sidecar_pump.rs` documents are exactly the ones worth pinning down and nothing currently tests them:

- one compl

ete JSON value per WS message, no framing
- **outbound frames carry no trailing newline** — the sidecar appends it

, so adding one puts a blank line into the agent's stdin
- a `

Binary` message is decoded as UTF-8, `Ping`/`Pong` ignored
- one unparseable frame is

logged and skipped rather than killing the session

That last pair is what `sends_raw`

exists for.

## But I'd hold off

Two reasons. `sidecar_pump.rs` is one of the unregistered files — it imports `domain::ports::Acp
Frames`, which no longer exists, so it can't be tested until it's ported to the new container port. And a real
test needs an actual `WebSocketStream` over `tokio::io::duplex` with a tungstenite handshake, which is a different we

ight of test from what we're building now.

So: the design *sh
ouldn't* block it, and right now it mildly does. I'd make `
next_outbound`/`deliver` public when we port the sidecar, rather than speculatively now — it's a two
-line visibility change plus moving the channel construction into `FakeAgent::new()`.
Want me to do that small restructure now anyway so the seam ex
ists, or leave it until the sidecar gets ported?

## Design intent (so you judge against the right goal)

These are test helpers for an agent-harness rewrite. The eventual test is an integration test that drives a session state machine by hand (no background pump task):
- `ContainerMock` is the `Transport<ToRuntimeMessage, ToServerMessage>` boundary. It owns a `FakeAgent`.
- `FakeAgent` is meant to represent the agent process and speak ONLY raw ACP (`RawJsonRpcMessage`), knowing nothing of the `agent-runtime.v0` envelope. The container does the envelope wrapping.
- `LogRepoMock` implements `agent_session::domain::ports::AgentSessionLogRepo` in memory.
- `transcript.rs` projects log entries into typed ACP enums for assertions.
- Goal was "typesafe all the way down": no hand-written ACP method-name string literals; use the `agent-client-protocol` crate's own enums and traits (`JsonRpcMessage::matches_method`, `parse_message`, `JsonRpcResponse`, `JsonRpcNotification`).

## What I want you to look for

Correctness and design bugs first, then quality:

- **Concurrency/locking**: `ContainerMock::recv` holds a `tokio::sync::Mutex` across `.await` inside `tokio::select!`. Is that sound? Is there a cancellation-safety problem — can a frame be LOST if the `select!` future is dropped mid-poll, or if `recv()` is cancelled? Does `UnboundedReceiver::recv` cancel safely here? Think hard about this one.
- **`std::sync::Mutex` used in async fns** (`FakeAgent`, `LogRepoMock`, `ContainerMock.outbound/events`). Held across await? Sound or not?
- **Shared-state cloning**: both mocks are `Clone` with `Arc` interiors. Is the sharing correct and complete? Is there any field that should be shared but isn't (or vice versa)?
- **`disconnects()`**: does it actually close the stream? It drops the events sender and calls `agent.close()`. Verify `recv()` can then return `Ok(None)`, and that the `select!` `else` branch fires correctly. Is there a bug where one channel closing but not the other causes a hang or a premature `None`?
- **Panics in helpers**: `transcript.rs` `parse()` and `TranscriptEntry::of` panic. Are the panic messages useful? Is panicking right here, or should it return Result? Is `expect("a response has an id")` reachable/unreachable?
- **`transcript.rs`**: is the `parse<T: JsonRpcMessage>` generic actually sound? Does passing `&Option<RawJsonRpcParams>` as `&impl Serialize` to `parse_message` produce the right JSON (does `None` serialize to `null` and break param parsing)? CHECK THIS by reading the acp crate source at ~/.cargo/registry/src/*/agent-client-protocol-1.2.0/src/jsonrpc.rs.
- **Dead/unused code**: `ContainerMock::sent()`, `FakeAgent::sends_raw`, `received_notifications`, `received_frames`, `LogRepoMock::entries` — are these used? Is `transcript()` even used yet? Is speculative unused API justified here or is it bloat?

1	//! The agent harness: one sandboxed coding agent session per request.
2	//!
3	//! The harness provisions a sandbox (today: Daytona, running the opencode
4	//! image under the service's `container/`), splices the sandbox harness's ACP
5	//! stream into agent_proxy's runtime link, and exposes an HTTP router for
6	//! starting and destroying sessions. It never speaks ACP itself: agent_proxy
7	//! owns the handshake, and every frame is relayed verbatim.
8	//!
9	//! Ports and adapters. [`domain`] owns the session use case and the ports it
10	//! needs; [`inbound`] is the HTTP trigger; [`outbound`] is Daytona plus the
11	//! Redis carrier for the upstream link. Nothing here reads the environment or
12	//! constructs its own adapters - that is the binary's job, in
13	//! `services/agent_harness_service`.
14	#![deny(missing_docs)]
15	// Every implementation below the ports is still `todo!()`, so the fields the
16	// adapters hold are written but never read. Comes out as they land.
17	#![allow(dead_code)]
18	
19	/// The session use case and the ports it needs.
20	pub mod domain;
21	pub mod inbound;
22	pub mod outbound;
23	/// Test doubles for the ports.
24	pub mod testing;
25	
26	/// Choose the TLS backend for this process.
27	///
28	/// Must be called before anything dials TLS. Both `ring` and `aws-lc-rs` end up
29	/// in this workspace's dependency graph - `aws-lc-rs` through the AWS SDK that
30	/// `kafka_util` pulls in for MSK IAM - so rustls refuses to pick one and panics
31	/// on first use instead. `reqwest` never trips this because it selects a
32	/// provider internally; the sidecar's WebSocket dial goes through
33	/// `tokio-tungstenite`, which does not.
34	///
35	/// Lives here rather than in the pump so the choice stays a process-level
36	/// decision the binaries make, but is written once so they cannot disagree.
37	/// Idempotent: a second call is a no-op rather than an error.
38	pub fn install_tls_provider() {
39	    // `Err` means a provider is already installed, which is the desired state.
40	    let _ = rustls::crypto::aws_lc_rs::default_provider().install_default();
41	}
42

content.text: There's the exact precedent — `frecency` does c

ross-crate mocks with a feature:

```toml
[features]
mock = ["dep:mockall"]
```
```rust
#[cfg_attr(feature

= "mock", mockall::automock)]   // ports.rs:115
```
and consumers opt in with `frecency = { path = "...

", features = ["mock"] }`.

So: **use mockall, don't hand-roll.** It handles RPITIT (`-> impl Future<..> + Send`) f
ine — `unfurl`, `properties`, `call` all do it. And `AgentSessionRepo` is easier than those: no associated `
Err` type (fixed `Result`), and every argument is owned (`AgentSessionId` is `Copy`, `New
AgentSession` owned), so you dodge the "explicit lifetime required by mockall's automock expansion" gotcha that `properties/ports.r

s:48` had to comment about.

One consolidation: I already added `test-utils = []` to `agent_session` for `
TEST_A`/`TEST_B`. Two features for one crate's test support is silly — I'd make it one,
`test-utils = ["dep:mockall"]`, gating both. And keep it in `agent_harness`'s `[dev-dependencies]` only, so a

plain `cargo build` never pulls mockall in.

## Now the wrapper — things worth ar

guing about

**Name.** "Manager" says nothing. What it actually owns is *liveness*. Your deleted proxy called this
`SessionRegistry` (`outbound/runtime_registry.rs`) — that's a better word, and there

's precedent in your own codebase.

**Three ports, one struct, no trait.**

```rust
pub struct S

Sessions,       // AgentSessionRepo
    logs: Logs,               // AgentSessionLogRepo
    live: Mutex<HashMap<AgentSessionId, Ar

c<Session>>>,
}
```

**`resume` should be idempotent, `create` shouldn't pretend to be.** Kafka is at-least-once, and
your old `inbound/kafka.rs` doc says the worker must dedupe on `message_id` before acting — so duplicate suppression is
the inbound adapter's job, not the registry's. But `resume` is naturally get-or-attach: already live → h
and back the existing session; not live → spawn a container and wire it. That asymmetry is worth making explicit in the names

, maybe `resume` vs `open`.

**Eviction is missing from every version
we've sketched.** `live` grows forever. A container dies, the pump exits, and the ent
ry stays. Your proxy had `handle_agent_detached` for exactly this. Either the registry gets `detach(id)`
, or the session unregisters itself when its stream ends — I'd prefer the former, since a session hol

ding an `Arc` back to its registry is a cycle.

**One log handle, not one per session.** You
said each session owns a log repo. If `Logs` is a postgres pool handle it's stateless, so "owns" means holds a clone —
and the session's own id is what scopes the writes. Which is the argument for the `NewLogEntry

` change from earlier: the session already knows its id, so making it restate it in every `AgentSessionLog` invites mismatch.

**
What `get` returns vs `create`.** `get` → `Option` (not live). `create`/`resume` → `Result` (it failed). Those are genu

inely different answers and shouldn't be collapsed into one.

Which of these do you want to push on first — the naming, or the `open`/`resume`
/`detach` shape?

response is the one it's waiting for — and per the earlier finding, a

lation explicit rather than hidden in an `.await`.

content.text: Good instinct — the `Mutex` is

there for a reason I didn't examine, and the reason is weak.

## Why I re

ached for it

`Transport::send(&self)` is `&self`, and the registry hands out `Arc<AgentSession>` to multiple callers. You
can't get `&mut` through an `Arc`. So the lock wasn't protecting anything con

ceptually shared — it was compensating for the `Arc` I'd already assumed.

## `&mut self` is better, and it

moves the concurrency somewhere honest

Make the state machine a plain single-owner struct:

```rust
pub struct AgentSession<C,

Logs> {
    id: AgentSessionId,
    container: C,
    logs: Logs,
    state: SessionState,          // plain field
    next_request_id: i

ut self, from: Option<..>, message: ToRuntimeMessage) -> Result<()>;
    pub async fn step(&mut self) -> Result<bool>;

pub fn status(&self) -> SessionStatus;      // &self, no lock
}
```

`Mutex` gone, `AtomicI64`

gone, `status()` can return whatever it likes because there's no guard to escape.

The
concurrency then lives in a thin wrapper rather than inside the state machine. One task owns the session; ever

yone else holds a cheap handle:

```rust
#[derive(Clone)]
pub struct SessionHandle {
    commands: UnboundedS

ender<Command>,
}
```

The registry stores `SessionHandle`, not `Arc<AgentSession>`. Production sp

awns a task that owns the session and selects between the container and the command channel.

## Why this is better for the thing we actually care about

The

test gets *simpler*, not harder:

```rust
let mut session = AgentSession::new(id
right — which is the most direct expression of "we don't pump for tests, we drive it by
hand." And `&mut self` makes it a compile error for two things to touch the state machine at

once, rather than a runtime lock that happens to serialize them.

It also removes a hazard I'd have had
to be careful about: with a `Mutex` inside, `send_message` must not hold the guard across the `container.send(..
).await`, or two senders deadlock-adjacent-

stall each other. `&mut self` makes that unrepresentable.

## The one real cost

`send
_message` through a handle becomes a channel send, so the caller no longer gets the state machine's `Result` syn
chronously. "Queued into the channel" and "the session accepted it" stop being the same event. If a
caller needs the real answer — e.g. the Kafka handler wants to know the session is
`Dead` rather than silently dropping a user's prompt — the command needs a `oneshot`

reply:

```rust
enum Command {
    Send { from: Option<..>, message: ToRuntimeMessage, reply: oneshot::Sender<Result<()>> },
}
```

That
's the price, and it's worth paying. It's also a smaller price than it looks, because with log-at-enqueue the dur

able record happens before the channel anyway.

## One thing to decide

With a single owning
task doing both jobs, `step()` can't just be "recv from container" — it has to select between the

container and the command channel. Two options:

- `step()` stays container-only, and the production `run()` loop does the `select!`, calling `send

_message` on the command branch. Tests keep using `step()` unchanged.
- `step()` takes the command receiver too

, so tests and production run identical code.

I'd take the first: tests drive `send_message` and `step`
directly, which is exactly the pair you asked for, and `run()` is ~15 untested lines of plumbing r

ather than a shape tests have to thread a channel through.

Want me to redo the
sketch with `&mut self` + `SessionHandle`, or go straight to building it?

content.text:
You're right on both, and the second one is more consequential than I'd realised.

##

Ids are automatic — the library has the whole machine

`SentRequest<T>` (`json
rpc.rs:3510`) holds `id`, `method`, a `oneshot::Receiver<ResponsePayload>`, and cancellation state. `ResponseRou
ter` (`:2751`) remembers the originating method and id so it can type the re
ply. So correlation, id minting, *and* cancellation are all done. Hand-rolling `next_request_id` +
`outstanding: RequestId` would be reimplementing JSON-RPC plumbing — the same mistake as writing `"session

/new"` by hand, one layer up.

That collapses the state machine substantially. It no longer needs ids at all:

```rust
enum SessionState {

Booting { pending: Vec<PendingSend> },
    Handshaking { pending: Vec<PendingSend>
king` just means "the handshake future is in flight". The handshake becomes `initialize(..).await` then `new_session(..).
await` — sequential, typed, correlated by the library. Our state machine owns only what

's genuinely ours: **the readiness gate and the buffer.**

## But there's a real tradeoff, and it h

its the testing story

To get that correlation you must drive ACP through the library's connection. `agent_runtime_protoc
ol` already exposes it — `ServerConnection::connect(channel, system_events)` returns a real `AcpChannel`
(`connection/mod.rs:59`) and splits system events off. That's what the deleted proxy used

.

The catch: `connect` does `tokio::spawn(run_server(..))`, and the library's own actors (`jsonrpc/
{incoming,outgoing,task}_actor.rs`) are more spawned tasks. So "
no pump in tests, drive everything by hand" partly goes away — you can't `step()` through a future
the library is driving. Tests become "do a thing, then await until the state chang

es", which needs timeouts and is less deterministic.

So:

| | hand-rolled ids | library connection |
|---|---|

---|
| correlation code | ~30 lines we own and must test | none |
| cancellation | we'd have

to build it | free |
| tests | fully deterministic `step()` | await-until, background tasks |
|

typed responses | we do the method→type mapping | free |

My lean is **the
library**, because reimplementing correlation to get nicer tests is optimising the wrong thing — and cancellation al
one (`session/cancel` on a user interrupt) is real work we'd otherwise owe. But it does
mean the integration test looks less like the sketch we've been iterating on, so it's your call.

## Either way, one helper change

The test can't assert `req(1)` — with the
library minting ids we don't know the value, and even with our own counter,

er the most recent request the harness sent.
pub fn replies_to_last(&self, response: impl JsonRpcResponse + Serialize);
```

That's
strictly better than `sends_reply(req(1), ..)` regardless of which path we take, and it's a small addition to what's

already there.

## And yes — assert on states

`status() -> SessionStatus` is `&self` with

no lock now, so:

```rust
assert_eq!(session.status(), SessionStatus::Booting);
container.s
ually pins the "ready ≠ sendable" behaviour, rather than inferring it from what didn't reach the agent.
Want me to look at how much of `ServerConnection` + the library's client surface we'd actually be ad
opting, so we can judge the determinism cost concretely before committing?

content.text: Two separate things, and I conflated them:
**`agent-client-protocol` 1.2.0 — external.** Plain crates.io dep (`Cargo.toml:106`), Zed's ACP SDK. Not
ours, can't change. But the part we want from it is just types
: `InitializeRequest`, `NewSessionRequest`, `RawJsonRpcMessage`, `JsonRpcMessage::method()`.
The part I was worried about — `SentRequest`, `ResponseRouter`, the `jsonrpc/*_actor.rs` machinery — is opt-in
. If we don't adopt its connection abstraction, those actors never spawn. So it's not a constraint, it's a men

u.

**`agent_runtime_protocol` — ours.** In-repo at `crates/agent_runtime_protocol`. Owns the v0 envelope (`ToServ
erMessage`/`ToRuntimeMessage`/`SystemEvent`/`AcpMessage`), the `Transport` port, `Channel`, the WebSocket car

rier, and `ServerConnection`/`RuntimeConnection`. Fully ours to reshape.

And the `t
okio::spawn` I flagged as a determinism cost was in **our** `ServerConnection::connect` — not the external crate.

## The useful finding

`ServerConnection` and `RuntimeConnection` now have **zero consumers.** `agent_proxy

` was the only one, and it's gone:

```
=== who still uses ServerConnection / RuntimeConnection ===
(n

othing outside agent_runtime_protocol itself)
```

So that whole abstraction — the one that spawns a driver task and splits system events from an
`AcpChannel` — is dead code we inherited a design constraint from. We're

not fighting a library; we're free to ignore it.

Which means the determinism worry basically evaporates. The re
served-id design needs none of it: `Container: Transport` gives us `recv()`/`send()`, and

`step()` drives the state machine directly. No spawned tasks anywhere in the tested path.

## What of ours we

actually still use

| module | status |
|---|---|
| `domain::schema::v0` | used — the

envelope, keep |
| `domain::ports::Transport` | used — `Container` builds on it |
| `outbound::websocket` | needed later

, for real containers |
| `testing::{fake_wire, wire_conformance}` | useful for the real car

rier |
| `domain::connection` | **dead** — `ServerConnection`/`RuntimeConnection` |
| `domain::channel` | only

used by `domain::connection` |

I'd leave the dead modules in place for now rather than widening
this change — but worth knowing they're not load-bearing, so if the
new design wants a differently-shaped connection helper, nothing is st
opping us. And if we never want one, that's ~200 lines pl

us its test file that can go.

So: nothing here is blocking. Ready to build the re
served-id version whenever you want to start.

content.text:
Straight answers:

**Mocks: no.** `agent-client-protocol-test` do
esn't exist on crates.io — it's an unpublished internal helper that leaks into their doc examples. What they *do* give you is `
Channel::duplex()` (`jsonrpc.rs:4411`), an in-memory connected pair. That's the test seam, just not adv

ertised as one.

**Nice ways to do things: yes, genuinely.** This is the part worth having:

```rust
let session = connection.build_session

t("fix the flaky test")?;
let update = session.read_update().await?;   // SessionMessage

```

`start_session()` (`session.rs:409`) performs the whole handshake. `ActiveSession` then exposes `session_id()
`, `send_prompt`, `read_update`, `read_to_string`, `modes()`. That deletes our `begin_handshake`,

the reserved ids, the response correlation — all of it.

**One thing you should know first: the crate is at 2.
0.0, we're pinned to 1.2.0.** If we're going to build on the high-level session API, I
'd resolve that gap before designing against a two-major-versions-old sh

ape.

## What adopting it actually requires

The library wants a transport implementing `ConnectTo<Host>` (
`Stdio`, `ByteStreams`, `Lines`, `Channel`). Our container doesn't speak raw ACP — it speaks the v0 envelope, where
`Event { AcpReady }` and `Acp(..)` are multiplexed on one stream. So we can't hand a

container to the library directly.

Something has to demux the envelope and surface the ACP substream. Which is *exactly* what our dead
`ServerConnection::connect` does — system events out one side, an ACP `Channel` out the other. So ad

opting the library means resurrecting and reshaping that, not deleting it.

## The division that falls out

It's act

ually clean, and it shrinks our state machine to almost nothing:

| layer | owner |

|---|---|
| envelope demux (Event vs Acp) | ours — reshaped `ServerCon

nection` |
| the `AcpReady` gate | **ours** — it's our protocol, not ACP |
| pending-prompt buffer | **

ours** — nothing in ACP knows about it |
| initialize / session/new / correlation / cancellation | library |
| pr

ompts and updates | library — `send_prompt` / `read_update` |

So `AgentSession` becom
es: buffer sends while booting → on `AcpReady`, hand the ACP substream to `
Builder` → `start_session()` → drain the buffer through `send_prompt`. `SessionState` collapses to roughly `Booting { p
ending } | Live(ActiveSession) | Dead`, with `Handshaking` folded inside the

library's `start_session().await`.

## The cost, restated concretely

`connect_with(transport, main_fn)` run
s handlers in the background and `into_connection_and_future` is private — so you can't drive the connection by

hand. Spawned tasks are inherent.

Tests stop being `step()`-driven. They become: sp
awn the harness side over `Channel::duplex()`, drive a fake agent on the other end, and await. Still controllable — the fake agent
decides when to reply — but you assert by awaiting a condition rather than stepping one frame at a time, which
means timeouts and a less exact "nothing happened yet" assertion. Los

ing the crisp `assert_eq!(status, Booting)` after a send is the specific regression.

## What

I'd suggest

The handshake code is small and the library's version is better — I'd take it

. But two things first, in order:

1. **Settle the 1.2.0 → 2.0.0 question**

, because designing against 1.2's `SessionBuilder` and then upgrading is wasted work.
2. **
Keep `FakeAgent` and `LogRepoMock`.** They surv
ive intact — `FakeAgent` already speaks only raw ACP, which is precisely what sits on the other end of a
`Channel::duplex()`. Only `ContainerMock`'s role changes: it stops being the ACP path

and becomes just the envelope carrier.

Want me to look at what changed in 2.0.0 first?

content.text: Confirmed the key
fact: **`impl<R: Role> ConnectTo<R> for Channel`** (`jsonrpc.rs:4437`). So a `Channel` is a valid transport — we can
hand the library our demuxed ACP substream directly. And `ConnectTo::into_channel_and_future()` is a public
trait method returning `(Channel, BoxFuture)`, so we can drive the connection future in our own `select!` rather than bl

ind-spawning.

Here's the change.

## What survives untouched

- `FakeAgent` — already

speaks only raw ACP, which is exactly what sits opposite a `Channel`
- `ContainerMock` — still the envelope carrier

; `sends_ready()` unchanged
- `LogRepoMock`, `transcript.rs`
- `Container: Transport<ToR

untimeMessage, ToServerMessage>`
- `AgentSessionRepo` / `AgentSessionLogRep

o`
- The `SessionRegistry` shape, `open`/`resume`/`get`/`detach`

## What chang

es

**1. New: envelope split (`agent_harness/src/domain/envelope.rs`)**

Turns a `Container` into the

ifecycle events to us, ACP frames to the library.
pub fn split<C: Container>(container: C) -> (UnboundedReceiver<SystemEvent>
don't want. Either reshape `agent_runtime_protocol::domain::connection` or write it here and

delete that module.

**2. `AgentSession` becomes an actor**

`ActiveSession`
is produced inside `connect_with`'s closure, so it can't be a struct field — it lives in a future. Which

forces the `SessionHandle` design we'd already converged on:

```rust
enum Command {
    Prompt { from

: Option<MacroUserIdStr<'static>>, text: String, reply: oneshot::Sender<Result<()>> },
    Status(oneshot::Sender<SessionStatus>),

fn run<C, Logs>(
    id: AgentSessionId,
    container: C,
    logs: Logs,
    stored: Option<AcpSessionId>,
    mut comm

acp, logs.clone(), id);          // see risk 1 below

    // Ours

```

`SessionState` collapses — `Handshaking` disappears entirely into `start_session().await`:

```rust
enum SessionStatus { Booting, Live, Dead }
```

**3. Deleted**

`begin_handshake`, the reserved id
constants, `on_frame` correlation, `acp_request`, `next_request_id`. Roughly the wh

ole state machine we've been designing, replaced by `start_session()`.

## Risks,

in order

**1. We stop seeing raw ACP frames — and the log is supposed to be source of truth
.** This is the one that needs designing, not just noting. Once the library owns the `Channel`,
