ixes the layering. Embedding the ACP id *inside* it, I'd push back on, for one specific reason:

**The ACP id doesn't
exist when the session id does.** The row is created at `NewSession`; the ACP id arrives when
`session/new` returns. So the field has to be `Option<AcpId>` — and then the same session has two *

unequal* `AgentSessionId` values across its life. That breaks it as a map key:

```rust
live.insert(id

_without_acp, session);   // registry inserts at open
live.get(&id_with_acp)                 // later lookup misses
```
`Eq`/`Hash` on an identity type that mutates mid-life is a landmine, and `HashMap<AgentSessionId, _
>` is exactly how the registry works today (`manager.rs:20`). It also costs `Copy`
— `AcpId(Arc<str>)` inside means no more `*id`, which ripples through every

call site.

Your own schema already separates them: `agent_session.id UUID PRIMARY KEY` and `acp_session_id` as a **n
ullable** column. And your deleted `AcpSessionId` doc said it outright — *"Never interchangeable with AgentId —

writing one where the other belongs addresses a message to a session that does not exist."*

## Same ergonomics without the hazard

```

rust
// agent_runtime_protocol — both protocol-level, both here so agent_session can

use them
pub struct AgentSessionId(Uuid);        // stays Copy, stable, map-key safe
pub stru

|')
```

You get `.acp_id()` and the `|` string form. The difference is that "ACP id not known
yet" becomes a type-level fact — you don't *have* a `SessionKey` until the handshake finishes — instead of an `Option` field
everyone has to remember to check. Which is also exactly the `Booting`/`Live` distinction the

state machine already encodes: `Live { key: SessionKey }`.

If you still want it on `AgentSessionId`
itself I'll build it that way — it's your call and it's rec
overable. But the map-key break would bite at runtime in the registry, not at compile time, so I wanted to name
it before writing it.

prompt.text: agent session key is good. but if we do this then can we also have on the kafka events that we modeled out earlier channelevent and newagentsession or whatever we  called htem -- use the session key? is that chill? to include in the events. this is coming together!

content.text: Tempting, but I'd say no — and for a reason that's

actually load-bearing rather than stylistic.

**A `SessionKey` only exists after the handshake.** The producer of `ChannelEvent` builds
it by reading the `agent_session` row, where `acp_session_id` is **nullable**. So the exact case we're building all
this buffering for — user posts a second message while the sandbox is still booting — is the case where the producer *can't* constru
ct a `SessionKey`. Putting it in the event makes the pre-handshake path unrepresentable, or forces it to `Option<AcpId>`, which pu

ts you back where we started.

**And it can go stale.** If resume turns out to mean a
fresh `session/new` rather than `session/load`, the ACP id changes. A `ChannelEvent` sitting in a partition would
carry a dead one. Kafka payloads are snapshots; ids that mutate make bad sn

apshots.

**Plus it leaks.** The ACP id is internal to the agent's conversation state. A channel-
message producer has no business knowing it, and once it's in an event schema, it's in ever

yone's schema.

So:

```rust
ChannelEvent {
    session: AgentSessionId,     // stable, always exists, saf

e to publish
    message_id: Uuid,
    channel_id: Uuid,
    kind: ChannelKind,
}
```

The harness resolves the r
est itself — and usually doesn't need to, because the live session already knows its own ACP id.

## Where `SessionKey` earns its keep

Exactly the places where "the handshake is done" is already

true:

- `SessionState::Live { key: SessionKey }` — the type makes it impossible to be `Live` without an ACP

id
- The translation fn — `AgentAction → ToRuntimeMessage`

needs `key.acp_id()`
- Anywhere addressing ACP, which is all post-handshake by definition

That's the n
ice part of the shape you landed on: `SessionKey` existing *
is* the proof the handshake completed, so no `Option` and no unwrap an

ywhere downstream. Events carry the stable id; the session carries the key.

So the ord
ering is: `AgentSessionId` + `AcpId` + `SessionKey` into `agent_runtime_protocol`, `error.rs`, then `action.rs` with the
translation and its test. Want me to go?

prompt.text: the acp id is 1:1 with the agent session id and will be needed to be persisted for resumption later though, right? maybe we just always query for it when we resume a session and don't bother using it in the key for now?
and we mutate the row in the db right after the session starts to set the acp id

content.text: Agreed, and that simplifies things further: **we
don't need to move `AgentSessionId` at all.** The only reason to relocate it was so a composite could h
old it. Without `SessionKey`, translation needs only `AcpId` → the library's `SessionId`

, so `AgentSessionId` stays in `agent_session` and there's no churn.

Two consequences of persisting on hand

shake completion:

**The session needs `AgentSessionRepo`, not just the log repo** — a third type param.
Which is fine, and it makes the integration test assert something real: that we

persisted the ACP id.

**`update(AgentSession)` is the wrong call for it.** Whole-row read-modify-write to set one field is rac

y if anything else touches the row. I'd add a narrow method:

```rust
fn set_acp_session_id(&self, id: AgentSessionId, acp

: &AcpId)
    -> impl Future<Output = Result<()>> + Send;
```

```rust

    Transport

impl<T> AgentConnector for T where

ct AgentSessionImpl<Connector> { id, connector }

## Why this is the right seam for the BYO case

The three things a
session actually does — buffer until ready, run the handshake, flush — need only `send`/`recv` of
the envelope. They don't need to know who booted the process. So your future path

drops in without touching any of that logic:

| | who spaw

ns | connector impl | has `ContainerId` |
|---|---|---|---|
| today | us

, via `ContainerManager` | `DaytonaContainer` | yes |
| BYO | them, on a webhook | an

inbound WS connection | no |

The BYO connector implements `Transport` over an
accepted WebSocket and is *not* a `Container` — nothing to reattach to, because we never provisioned it. `
ContainerManager` simply isn't involved; something else parks the connection and hands it to a

session. The buffering and flushing are reused verbatim, which is what you wanted.

That also means `AcpReady` ke
eps working unchanged for BYO: their sidecar emits it when their agent is wired up, same

as ours.

## One consequence worth noting

`ContainerManager` is now only reachable on the *spawn* path,
not the session path. So when we write the registry it'll need two entry points — `open`
/`resume` (we provision) and something like `attach` (they connected to us) — conver
ging on the same `AgentSession::new`. Worth designing the registry with that in mind rather than assuming every

session came from a `ContainerManager`.

Nothing else is blocking. The remaining plumbing before
the state machine is unchanged: mockall on `agent_session`, `set_acp_session_id`, and `acp_session_id: Option<String>
` → `Option<AcpId>`. Want me to do that and then write it?

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Bring a booted sandbox to "ready", idempotently.
#
# Run by `agent_harness::domain::provision::ensure_ready_command`, which embeds
# this file with `include_str!`. Every stage skips itself when already done, so
# this is safe on first boot, on reconnect, and after a machine restart.
#
# The paths below are properties of the container image (see the service's
# `container/Dockerfile`), not configuration, which is why they live here rather
# than in Rust. The one value Rust also needs is the sidecar port, because it
# has to dial the sidecar afterwards - `provision::SIDECAR_PORT` mirrors it and
# a test asserts the two agree.
#
# REPO_URL and GITHUB_TOKEN come from the sandbox environment, set at creation.
# They are never interpolated into this script.
set -e

workspace_dir=/workspace
sidecar_port=8700
# Macro dev shell baked into the image at build time; absent on images built
# without the github_token secret.
repo_env_file=/env/repo-dev-env.sh
sidecar_log=/tmp/acp-sidecar.log

# 1. Credentials, so the clone below can read a private repo.
gh auth setup-git --hostname github.com --force

# 2. The repo, unless it is already cloned.
if [ ! -d "$workspace_dir/.git" ]; then
  git clone --depth 1 "$REPO_URL" "$workspace_dir"
fi

# 3. The sidecar, unless it is already answering. The baked dev shell goes
#    first on PATH, with the image's own tools (opencode, gh) still reachable
#    behind it.
#
#    Checked explicitly because `nohup ... &` backgrounds the process, so its
#    failure is invisible to `set -e` - a missing binary would otherwise show up
#    only as a readiness timeout a minute later, with nothing to point at it.
if [ ! -x /opt/acp-sidecar ]; then
  echo "no executable /opt/acp-sidecar in this image; was it built into it?" >&2
  exit 1
fi

if ! curl -sf "localhost:$sidecar_port/ping" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  baked_path="$PATH"
  if [ -f "$repo_env_file" ]; then
    # shellcheck disable=SC1090
    source "$repo_env_file"
    export PATH="$PATH:$baked_path"
  fi
  nohup /opt/acp-sidecar >"$sidecar_log" 2>&1 &
fi

`MockContainerManager::spawn` drops its `format!("sandbox-{session}")` in favour of `ContainerMock::new(session.into())`. Tests green.

The real payoff is

prompt.text: why option?

content.text: `Ok(None)` means the connector closed — it's `Transport`'s contract, not a cho

ice made here. From `agent_runtime_protocol/src/domain/ports.rs:26`:

> Returns `Ok(None

)` once the counterpart has closed the connection.

So the three cases are: `Ok(Some(msg))` a message
arrived, `Ok(None)` the sandbox went away cleanly, `Err(..)` the carrier it
self failed. Distinguishing the middle from the last matters — a st

opped sandbox is normal and resumable, a broken socket isn't.

That said, **`receive()` dis
appears with the state machine.** It's the old pass-through API. Once `step()` exists, the `Option` is consumed intern
Ok(false)` to the caller, so nothing outside the session ever sees an `Option`. Same for `send`/`rece
ive` generally — they're both replaced by `send_message(AgentAction)` and `step()`.

content.text: State
machine and integration test are in, both green, and m

utation-checked.

## `SessionState`

```rust
enum SessionState {
    Booting { pending: Vec<AgentAction> },

Handshaking { pending: Vec<AgentAction> },
    Live { acp: AcpId },
    Dead,
}
```

`&mut self`, no `Mutex`, no
`Arc`, no spawned tasks. `status() -> SessionStatus` is a payload-free snapshot so tests can
assert transitions. `send_message(AgentAction)` queues in `Booting`/`Handshaking`, translates-and-sends in `Live
`, errors in `Dead`. `step()` handles one inbound message and returns `false` when the stream ends; `pump()` is the three-line unt

ested loop.

Handshake uses reserved ids (`agent_harness:initialize`, `agent_harness:session/new`) so they can't collide with a
caller's, pipelined as your proxy did. Prompts get `agent_harness:prompt:N` from a pl

ain `u64`. Both directions are logged through `AgentSessionLogRepo`.

## The test

Asserts the full transition sequence — `Booting → Handshaking →
Live → Dead` — plus at each point what did and didn't reach the agent, and that the log
captured 8 entries in wire order. Typed throughout: `[ClientRequest::In

itializeRequest(_), ClientRequest::NewSessionRequest(_)]`, no method strings.

## Mutation-checked, and it caught me

out

I ran two deliberate breakages. Removing the queue drain failed the test, as expected. But making
the handshake fire on **any** `SystemEvent` instead of just `AcpReady` **passed** — the test only ever sent `Acp

Ready`, so nothing proved the gate existed. That's the single most important behaviour in the whole thing.

Added the
missing assertion (an unrelated `SystemEvent::Unknown` must leave it `Booting`

with nothing sent), and both mutations now fail. Worth knowing the original test had that hole.

## Two things I deliberately left

out

**Persisting the ACP id.** You wanted the row mutated right after `session/new`
returns. That needs `AgentSessionRepo::set_acp_session_id`, which means a new sqlx query and
a `just prepare_db` run — and per your notes a failed prepare w
ipes the whole `.sqlx` cache with the devshell pointing at a dead database. I didn't want to
risk that inside this change. The session exposes `acp_id()` and the hook goes in `
go_live`; it's a small follow-up once we're ready to touch s

qlx.

**`session/load` on resume.** Punted as agreed — container-level resume works and

is tested, ACP-level resume isn't wired.

One warning left: `AgentSession`
/`SessionStatus` unused in the lib target since only tests use them. Goes away with the registry.

now the test hand-wires `spawn` + `AgentSession::new`, which is exactly what `open()` will do, so if the
real wiring differs the test won't notice. Going through the manager buys that co

verage.

But there's a conflict to settle first.

## The registry can't both

own sessions and let tests `step()` them

We built the session as `&mut self`, single-owner. A registry that stores sessions so `get(id)` works

owns them, and can't hand out `&mut`. So either:

**A. `open()` h
ands over ownership.** Returns `AgentSession` by value; it does *not* spawn a pump or
register anything. The caller owns it. Production then separately spawns a task that owns the session and registers a `SessionHandle` in

the registry's `live` map.

```rust
let mut session = registry.open(new_session).await?;   // test drives this directly
```

**B.
Registry owns, exposes only handles.** Tests can't `step()` — they'd need the pump running and would
assert by awaiting-until, losing the deterministic stepping we just built and

mutation-verified.

I'd take **A**. It preserves everything from this
round, and it keeps the registry honest: it's a directory of *live hand
les*, not a container of state machines. The split is `open()` = "build and wire",

`spawn_pump()` = "start driving and register".

It also fits the BYO case — an inbound conn
ection has no `ContainerManager`, so `attach(connector)` becomes a third

constructor alongside `open`/`resume`, all converging on `AgentSession::new`.

##

Which mocks we actually need

**No mock manager.** This is where the earlier "no manager trait" dec
ision pays off: the test builds a *real* registry over mock ports and asserts on those. A `MockSessionRegistry` would only let you

assert "someone called open", which is a tautology.

**We do need `MockAgentSessionRepo`**
, because `open()` calls `create(NewAgentSession)` to mint the row. Good news: `create` already exists on the trait, so **
this needs no new SQL and no `prepare_db` run** — the sqlx risk I dodged earlier doesn't apply. It

's just mockall wiring on `agent_session`, following `frecency`'s pattern:

```toml
test-utils = ["d

ep:mockall"]

```rust

Keep `LogRepoMock` hand-rolled.** `MockAgentSessionLogRepo` would work, but our version
has `entries()`, and asserting "8 entries in w

ire order" through mockall expectations is much worse than reading a `Vec`.

**Nothing needed in `agent.rs`.
** `FakeAgent` sits below the container and is unaffected — the registry hands you

a container, and its agent is reachable via `containers.container(id).agent()`.

smaller things

**Name.** You said "agent session manager"; I'd been writing `SessionRegist

now |

## `AgentSessionManager` — no containers

```rust
pub struct AgentSess

ogRepo
}

pub async fn create(&self, new: NewAgentSession) -> Result<AgentSessionRecord>
pub async fn get(&self, id: AgentSess

ionId) -> Result<AgentSessionRecord>
pub fn attach<Connector: AgentConnector>(&self, id, connector) -> A

gentSession<Connector, Logs>
```

Two ports, no `ContainerManager` anywhere. It mints rows and wires s

essions; each session owns its own state machine and the manager holds none.

**It came out two-phase,
and that's forced rather than chosen.** `ContainerId: From<AgentSessionId>` means a link is named after the session it serves —
so the row must exist before anything can be provisioned. Hence `create` → (someone provisions) → `attach`. That's exactly the se

reviewed.

## Also landed

`agent_session
` now has `test-utils = ["dep:mockall"]` with `#[cfg_attr(feature = "test-utils", mockall::automock)]`
on both port traits, following `frecency`'s pattern. The test uses `MockAgentSessionRepo` with `expect_create().times(1)`, so it pro

ves the row is actually minted rather than assumed.

## Two name collisions worth knowing about

`agent_session::domain::model` exports both `Agent
Session` **and** `SessionStatus`, and we now have our own of each. In the test they
're imported as `AgentSessionRecord` and `RecordStatus`. It compiles fine, but any
new file touching both will hit the same thing — worth considering renaming ours (or the

irs) at some point rather than aliasing at every call site.

## Remaining

Three unused-import warnings, all "only
used in tests" — they clear once something in the lib w
ires the manager up. And still outstanding from earlier: `set_acp_session_id` (needs new SQL + `
prepare_db`), and ACP-level resume via `session/load`.

content.text: Tr
immed to two tests in `agent/test.rs`, and both earn their place — breaking the

handshake tracking fails both.

## What `FakeAgent` now enforces

`deliver` checks
ACP ordering and panics rather than recording, tracking a three-stage `Fresh → Initialized → SessionOpen
` progression. `SessionOpen` is reached when the agent *answers* the `session/new` it

received — not when it receives it, which is the distinction that matters.

- `initialize` → advances to `Initialized`
-
`session/new` / `session/load` → panics if still `Fresh` ("before initialize"); remembers the

request id
- anything else → panics unless `SessionOpen` ("before its ACP session existed")

So the harness s
ending a prompt too early is now a loud failure at the point of the mistake, not a silent rec

ording that some later assertion might or might not notice.

The two tests: the happy order is accepted, and the subtle one — `initialize`
sent *and* `session/new` sent but **not yet answered** — panics. I dropped the c
ruder "prompt with nothing sent at all" and "session/new before initialize" cases; they're the

same rule with less to say.

## Also in this round

**Inlined `pr
ompt()` and `reserved()`** in `agent_sessions/tests.rs` — 7 `AgentAction::Prompt(

AgentPromptAction { .. })` literals at their call sites now.

**Repl
aced both `.len()` assertions with real content assertions.** `ClientRequest` has no `PartialEq`, so inst

ead of counting I destructure an exhaustive slice pattern and assert the payloads:

```rust
let [
    ClientRequest::Initialize

assert_eq!(flushed.prompt, vec![ContentBlock::from("fix the flaky
ries **the right ACP session id and the right text** — i.e. the queued action was translated correctly, not just that *

a* prompt appeared. Same for the second, live-path prompt.

content.text: Yes for the two ids — and one of them is barely used.

`WORKSPACE` is a different problem.

## `INITIALIZE_ID` — nothing correlates it
`on_frame` only ever matches `NEW_SESSION_ID`; the `initialize` response is discarded. So the constant exists pur

ely so the *test* can reply to it. It doesn't need to be public, or a constant at all.

(Separate
observation: we don't check the agent's `protocolVersion` against ours. Worth doing e

ventually, and that's the only reason to correlate the initialize response.)

## `NEW_SESSION_ID` — store the id

instead of reserving one

The reason for a well-known id is that `on_frame` needs to rec

ognise the response. But it could just *remember what it sent*:

```rust
Handshaking {
    pending: Vec<

AgentAction>,
    opened: RequestId,   // the id we minted for session/new
}
```

Then `on_frame` compares against
`opened`, and the id can be anything — a counter value, a uuid, whatever. Both constants dis

appear from the public surface.

The blocker was that the test needs to know the id to reply. But **`FakeAg
ent` already tracks it** — the protocol enforcement I just added stores `progress.opening`
id named anywhere. That's also *more* faithful: the agent replies to what it actually received rather than what the test assumed it

would receive. Same trick for initialize if we ever correlate it.

Net: two

`pub const`s gone, one field added, one helper added, test reads better.

## `WORKS

PACE` is genuinely coupled and can't just be deleted

It's
duplicated already — `container/ensure_ready.sh` has `workspace_dir=/workspace`, and the script
's own header says these paths are *"properties of the container image, not configuration"*. So the two

can silently disagree.

Three options, and the right one depends on where you think the tru

th lives:

- **The connector reports it.** `AgentConnector::workspace()` — the connector is the thing that knows what filesystem is on the other end

, and a BYO container reports its own. Most correct, costs a port method.
- **The session record carries it.** `N
ewAgentSession` already has `repo_url`; a `workspace` beside it is per-session config. Cheap, but it's not really

per-session.
- **Leave it, and add a test that the Rust constant matches the script.** That
's what `provision::SIDECAR_PORT` did — there was a test asserting the constant and

the script agreed. Restores the guarantee without moving anything.

I'd do
the third now (cheap, kills the real risk) and the first when the BYO crate lands, since that

's when "whose workspace?" actually becomes a question.

Want me to do the id remov
al now, and leave `WORKSPACE` with a conformance test?

ness hasn't sent the corresponding request. This is strictly more faithful than before — the agent answers **what it actually received**

content.text: Both cons
`super`; the test picks them up via its existing `use super::*`, so the version literal is gone from both sides — the session
sends `InitializeRequest::new(PROTOCOL_VERSION)` and the fake agent answers `InitializeResponse::new(PROTOCOL_VERSION)`.

Bumping the version is now one line, and the test moves with it.

6 tests green. Same three "

only used in tests" warnings as before.

Worth noting for later: because the test echoes `PROTOCOL_VERSION` back
, it can't catch a *mismatch* — we still don't validate the agent's reported version against
ours. That's the gap I mentioned when deleting `INITIALIZE_ID`: correlating the `initialize`
response is what would let us reject an agent speaking a different version. Cheap to add if you want it.

content.text: Yes — it hel

ps in two ways.

**`JsonRpcMessage::to_untyped_message()`** does the serialize *and* carries the method name,
so `UntypedMessage::into_parts()` hands back exactly the `(method, params)` pair `RawJsonRpcMessage

::request` wants. No `serde_json::to_value` and no `.method().to_owned()` at the call site.

**`ag
ent_client_protocol::Error` implements `std::error::Error`**, so a `#[from]` variant on `HarnessError` lets `?` do the work —
all four `map_err(|error| HarnessError::Container(error.to_string()))` calls are gone, along with the m

islabelling (those weren't container failures).

Per request: 5 lines → 3,

and nothing hand-rolled.

One thing the library *won't* give us: `UntypedMessage::into_ra
w_jsonrpc_message(id)` does exactly the last step, but it's `pub(crate)`. So the `RawJsonRpc

Message::request(method, params, id)` line stays ours. Not worth working around.

`action.rs
` in `agent_runtime_protocol` still has the older hand-rolled form for the same job — same tre

atment would apply there (its `ActionError::Acp(String)` could become a `#[from]`), if you want it consistent.

6 tests
green.

content.text: User

id is threaded and verified.

## How it flows

`send_message
` takes it, and the buffer carries it — because *when

the action arrives* is the only time it's knowable:

```rust
pub struct PendingAction

{
    pub from: Option<MacroUserIdStr

<'static>>,
    pub action: AgentAction,
}

pub async fn send_message(&mut self, from: Option<MacroUserIdStr<'static>>,

action: AgentAction)
```

`log(user_id, content)` and `send_now(from, message)` carry it down. Handshake frames and inbound tra

ffic pass `None`.

The test now sends as a real user and asserts the log entry for the *flushed* prompt is attributed to them — which is the wh
ole point, since the action reached the wire long after the request that created it. Mutation-checked: replacing `queued.from` with `None

` on flush fails the test.

**Worth flagging:** my first attempt at that assertion silently didn't apply — `cargo fmt`
had reflowed the line I was patching against, so the replacement matched nothing and the test still passed. The mutation check is

the only reason I caught it. Fixed and re-verified.

## On `send_success` / replay

Not h
ard, but it needs a migration, so I've only shaped it. `send_now
` already logs **before** sending, so a message that never left the box is recorded — the ordering that

makes replay possible is in place, with a comment saying so.

What's still missing is three

things that travel together:

1. A column — `sent_at T
IMESTAMPTZ NULL` (better than a bool: tells you *when*, and N

ULL is the unsent case)
2. `AgentSessionLogRepo::create` returning the
entry id, so there's something to mark. It already generates a `uuid_v7` internally, so **no new S

QL** for that part.
3. `mark_sent(entry_id)` — this is the part

needing new SQL + `prepare_db`.

The one design note:
give `mark_sent` a **default no-op body** on the trait rather than `todo!()`. Then the postgres impl inherits a har
mless no-op until the migration lands, the mock overrides it to record, and the session can call it today without a `

todo!()` panic waiting in production.

Replay then becomes: on start, `list
_by_session` where `direction = 'to_runtime' and sent_at is
null`, re-send oldest first. That's the durable-buffer property the deleted `agent_proxy_pending_message` table had

, without a second table.

Say when and I'll do it — it's the nat
ural pairing with `set_acp_session_id`, since both are one migration.

content.text: Su
spicion confirmed. Honest answer: I feel good about the *shape*

, less good about a few specifics.

## What I'd defend

The
state machine is small, single-owner, lock-free, task
-free, and **mutation-tested** — four separate deliberate breakages (drop-action, never-drain, wrong-
correlation, lose-user-on-flush) all fail the test. That's the part I tr

ust, because it's been actively attacked rather than just written.

`FakeAgent` enforcing
ACP ordering is the best thing here. It already caught that the old test was
sending `session/prompt` as a *notification*, which no amount of string-comparison assertion would have no

ticed.

And the pushback you gave twice — "why are
we touching wire names", "the library must do this" — was right both times, and the result is that there's

now not one ACP method literal in the crate.

## What I don't feel good about

**1
. A refused handshake wedges the session.** `on_frame` returns `Err` when `session/new` com
es back an error, but nothing sets `Dead` — the only path to `Dead` is stream end (`session.rs
:135`). So the session sits in `Handshaking` forever with a live connector, buffering prompts that will never send

, while `pump()` has already aborted. That's a genuine bug, not a gap, and it's untested.

**2.
Nothing is wired, so every assumption is unvalidated.** No production call site for anything we've built. Does the real s
idecar actually emit `AcpReady`? Does pipelining `initialize` + `session/new` work against opencode, or does it reject the
second before answering the first? Is `/workspace` right? All of that is currently a guess dressed up in

types.

**3. Resume doesn't work, and it *looks* like it does.** Container-level resume is
implemented and tested — but `acp_session_id` is never written to the row, so there's nothing to resume *into*. `Mock

ContainerManager::resume` passing green is slightly misleading about the state of the feature.

**4. `H
arnessError::Container` is a dumping ground.** It's carrying JSON errors and "the agent refused session/new", neither of which is

a container failure. Should be `Handshake`/`Protocol` variants.

**5. We deleted 3,790
lines of working code and haven't replaced its function.** `agent_proxy` did a job in production; nothing does that
job now, and its infra is still deployed. That's fine as a deliberate mid-refactor state, but it shouldn't dr

ift out of view.

Smaller: the pending buffer is unbounded; `step()` logs before dispatch so a log failure dr
ops an already-consumed frame; a second `AcpReady` is guarded but untested; the test has four near-identical `

pending()` assertion blocks.

## What I'd do next

Fix #1 — it's small
and it's a real bug. Then wire *one* real thing end to end (probably
Daytona + the WebSocket carrier against a live sandbox) before building more on
top, because that's what converts assumptions #2 into facts. #3 and #4 are cheap and can
ride along with the migration.

## The trade-off

Today the enum makes "`
Live` implies an empty buffer" unrepresentable — `pending()` returns `&[]` for `Live`. With a separate field, a bug *

ather than by type. Moving the field doesn't remove a check, it just stops the type from impl

` after the drain, or a test asserting `pending()` is empty once live — which the integ

than what I proposed. Clone the buffer out and the whole problem evaporates, without restructuring an
- **`&self.state`, not `&mut`.** The borrow is immutable and ends at the clone, so nothing down

stream conflicts.
- **No `mem::take`, no `unreachable!()`.** The destructure that gets `pending` is
the *same* one that checks `opened`, so there's only one match and it's the one that already

had to happen.
- **Keeps the invariant.** `pending` stays inside the enum, so `Live` still can

't carry a buffer. My proposal traded that away for no good reason.

The cost is one `
Vec<PendingAction>` clone, once per session, on the handshake-completion path — a few
queued prompts with a `String` each. Against a Daytona sandbox boot it's not

measurable.

And it only clones when the frame *is* the `session/new` answer, since the id check comes first.

Same
shape works in `go_live` if you'd rather keep it as a function, but in
lined it's better still: one match serves both the id check and the drain, and the refused-handshake path

gets its `Dead` transition right next to the success path.

content.text: We
don't — and that's a bug in both versions, including the one on disk right

now.

`mem::take` empties the buffer up front, then the drain loop does `self.send_now(..).await?`. If the third of five que
ued actions fails to send, the `?` returns and **the remaining two are gone** — they only existed in the local `Vec` that just

got dropped. Cloning has exactly the same hole.

So your question kills my "the field split is
n't worth it" answer. It *is* worth it, for correctness rather than tidiness: the buffer has to outlive the state transition,

and it can't if it's stored inside the state we're replacing.

content.text: Set

up, and all three new behaviours are mutation-verified.

##

What changed in the session

**Buffer moved out of `SessionState`** into its own `VecDeque<P
endingAction>` field, so it survives a state transition. `Booting` and `Handshaking` no longer duplicate a `pending` field — `Hand

shaking` carries only `opened`.

**Drain peeks, then pops after success:**

```

**`send_message` in `Live` flushes first**, so a new action can't overtake a stranded one — which also makes rec

overy automatic rather than needing a retry path.

**`go_live` inlined into `on_fr
ame`**, and a refused `session/new` now sets `Dead` instead of leaving the session wedged in `Handshaking` forever. New `HarnessError::

Handshake` variant, since those weren't container failures.

## Test infrastructure

`ContainerMock::fails_sends_after(count
)` — one `Arc<Mutex<Option<usize>>>` budget checked at the top of `send`. And

`FakeAgent::refuses_session(error)`, which errors the `session/new` it actually received.

## Two new tests

**`a_fail
ed_flush_strands_the_remainder`** — queues three prompts, lets two through, fails the third. Asserts
the third is still queued (not dropped), then that a fourth action flushes it *first

*, so the agent receives `first, second, third, fourth` in order.

**`a_refused_handshake_kills_the_session`** — agent errors `

session/new`; session goes `Dead` and further sends fail.

## Mutations, all caught

| mutation | result |
|---

|---|
| `mem::take` instead of peek-then-pop | FAILED |
| no `Dead` on refusal | FAILED |
| no flush-before-send in

`Live` | FAILED |

8 tests green. Same three "only used in tests" warnings.

Ready to cut this
into commits for the branch — want me to go ahead?

prompt.text: but also we're doing all the handshake style logic manually. is there a way we could have the library do it for us or is that a bad idea? or use their types?

content.text: We're already using their types throughout — `InitializeRequest`, `NewSessionRequest`, `NewSessionResponse`, `ClientRequest`,
`RequestId`, `ContentBlock`, and `to_untyped_message()` which removed the last hand-written serialization. There's no method string

left in the crate. So that half is done.

What's still ours is **sequencing and correlation**, and it's sm

aller than it feels:

- mint an id (`next_id`)
- remember it (`

Handshaking { opened }`)
- compare the response against it
- `serde_json::from_value::<NewSessionRes

ponse>`

That's about 15 lines of actual logic. The rest of `begin_handshake` is just building two typed requests.

## The library

would replace it, at a price we already rejected

`
ConnectionTo::build_session(cwd).start_session()` does `initialize` + `session/new` and hands back an `ActiveSession`. But get
ting there needs, as before: an envelope demux to produce a `Channel`, `
connect_with` spawning actors, and **a tee so the log still sees raw frames** — that last one being the real

risk, since `read_update()` only surfaces session updates, not every request/response.

Concretely, ad
opting it now would delete ~40 lines and add ~60, and cost the `step()` determinism that
all 8 tests and every mutation check depend on. That's a bad trade for the handshake al

one.

## The thing that should tip it later: cancellation

A user interrupting a turn means `session/cancel`, plus c
ancelling the in-flight `session/prompt`. The library has that built in — `SentRequest` carries `RequestCanc
ellation`, `forward_cancellation_from`, and `is_cancel_request_notification`. Hand-rolling *that* is a genuinely b

ad idea in a way that hand-rolling a two-request handshake isn't.

So my read: **keep it manual now, and when
cancellation lands, adopt the library connection wholesale** rather than piecemeal. Piecemeal is the worst option — you'd car

ry both the demux/tee complexity and the hand-rolled correlation.

One caveat on my own recommendation: I haven't verified `
start_session()` works over a plain `Channel` in 1.2.0, only that `Channel` implements `ConnectT
o`. If we ever seriously consider it, that's the first thing to pr
ove with a spike — and it's also when the 1.2.0 → 2.0
.0 gap needs settling, since the session API is where the majors lik

ely diverge.

Nothing to change today unless you want me to spike it. Otherwise I
'll cut the commits.

rawInput.command:
git commit -q -m "$(cat <<'EOF'
refactor(agent_harness): rebuild around an agent session state machine

Replaces the proxy-splicing design with a session that owns the ACP
handshake itself. One commit because it is one swap: the old ports and the
new ones cannot both be in the module tree.

The session is &mut self with no locks, tasks or channels, so tests drive
it a message at a time through step() and no pump runs. It queues actions
until the container reports AcpReady, sends initialize and session/new,
and flushes only once session/new answers with an AcpId - "ready" means
handshakeable, not sendable, which is the bug this shape exists to
prevent.

The queue lives outside SessionState so a flush that fails part-way leaves
the remainder queued rather than dropping it with the old state, and
sending while live flushes first so nothing overtakes a stranded action. A
refused session/new kills the session instead of wedging it in
Handshaking.

AgentConnector is the port the session talks to, so a container someone
else spawns and dials into us later reuses all of the above unchanged;
Container only adds the sandbox identity needed to reattach.
AgentSessionManager mints rows and plugs links into sessions, and knows
nothing about containers - provisioning is a separate crate's job, done by
hand in tests until it exists.

Test helpers: FakeAgent speaks raw ACP only and panics if the harness
speaks out of order, which caught a prompt being sent as a notification.
ContainerMock is the envelope boundary and can refuse sends on demand.
Every behaviour here was checked by mutating the source and confirming the
tests fail.

Not yet wired: no production caller, acp_session_id is never persisted, and
ACP-level resume via session/load is unimplemented.
EOF
)" && git log --oneline -4

ktree clean, all four verified to build and 32 tests green at `HEAD`.

| commit | what |
|---|---|
|

`349b2df9b` | `chore:` remove the agent proxy crate and service — 31 files, −4,158 |
| `6f670a0

e2` | `feat(agent_runtime_protocol):` `AcpId` + `AgentAction` with ACP translation |
| `56dececb2` | `

feat(agent_session):` `test-utils` feature (mockall ports, test ids, `Display`) |
| `5aff783ca` | `refactor(agent_harness):` r

ebuild around the session state machine |

The split is by crate and by concern, and the first three are independent — each buil

ds standalone, so the sequence bisects cleanly.

**The fourth is large (27
files) and I couldn't split it.** `domain/mod.rs` can't list the old ports and the new ones at once, so the deletions and the additions are one
atomic swap. Splitting further would have meant artificial intermediate states that don't compile — wor

se than one honest commit. Its message says why.

Two things to know:

- **`Carg
o.lock` is in the last commit only.** It carries all the dependency changes cumulatively (proxy removal plus `thiserror`
/`macro_user_id`/`mockall` on the harness). Checking out commit 1 alone would have cargo regenerate it — harmless, but it's why

the lock isn't split.
- **It includes your pre-existing uncommitted work**, not just mine: the deletions of `domain/{handler
,ports,provision,runtime}.rs` and `testing/mock_proxy.rs` were already in the worktree when we started,

and they belong to this same swap.

Untouched and still outstanding, as the first commit's message records: the de
ployed Pulumi stack and Doppler project, the applied `agent_proxy_pending_message` migration, the SDK's `ag

ent-proxy` entry, and the generated web client.

Nothing is pushed. Want me to push to `wolf/system-ai-
agents`?
